instance: $root
instance: BIT2
END my_program.exe

%>

Basic NPI Program Architecture
The following example shows the basic construct of an NPI program:
(include other header files)
// 1. include header files for NPI
include "npi.h" // a must-have for NPI programs
include "npi_hdl.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI
Language-SystemVerilog model
include "npi_nl.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI Netlist model
include "npi_dm.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI DM model
include "npi_text.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI Text model
include "npi_fsdb.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI FSDB model

{
// 2. parse the user-specific arguments for the program

int npi_argc;
char** npi_argv;
parse_arguments(argc, argv, npi_argc /*Output*/,
npi_argv /*Output*/);
// 3. initialize NPI models
if( !npi_init(npi_argc, npi_argv) )
// 4. if you'd like to use NPI Language/Netlist/DM/Text model,
npi_load_design is a must
if( using_npi_language_or_netlist_or_dm_or_text_model() )
npi_load_design(npi_argc, npi_argv);
(your NPI procedures)
// 5. end of NPI models
}

A typical NPI program contains the following 5 sections:
1. Include the NPI header files.
2. Separate the arguments for NPI from those for your program.
3. Initialize NPI.
4. Load the design if necessary.
5. End NPI.

Include Files
The header file: npi.h should always be included for an NPI program while including the
other NPI header files based on the models to be used.
Refer to the following for the mapping between the header files and the NPI models:
* npi_hdl.h: NPI Language model.
* npi_nl.h: NPI Netlist model.
* npi_dm.h: NPI Design Manipulation (DM) model.
* npi_text.h: NPI Text model.
* npi_fsdb.h: NPI FSDB model.
* npi_fsdb_trans.h: NPI FSDB model for transaction FSDB.

Parsing Arguments in the NPI Program
Typically, the usage of an NPI program is similar to the following:
%> my_NPI_program.exe <verdi import design options> <NPI options> <user
options>

where <novas import design options> might include the following common options. Other
<novas import design options> can be listed by "novas -h".
Table 1

Novas Import Design Options

title: Appendix 2274
text: Specify the design file (for example, *.f) to be imported.

title: Appendix 2274
text: Specify the design library name (for example, work.lib++/).

title: Appendix 2274
text:
-path pathname Specify the path of the design file (*.f) or design library
(work.lib++).
-top topModule Specify the top module of the design library.
-verilog

title: Appendix 2274
text:
Specify the Verilog language type for the imported files (for
example, *.v).

title: Appendix 2274
text:
Specify the SystemVerilog language type for the imported
files (for example, *.sv).

<NPI options> are for NPI models. Refer to the following section for details. You need to
separate user-defined arguments from <verdi import design options> and <NPI options>.
For example, pick up "-input_signal system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode" in the following
command line:
%> my_program_arg.exe -lib work -top system -input_signal
"system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode"

The following code snippet demonstrates how this can be achieved:

{
// 2. parse the user-specific arguments for the program
string input_signal; // use STL string
int npi_argc = 0;
char** npi_argv = (char**) malloc(sizeof(char*)*argc);
for(int i=0; i<argc; i++) {
if( strcmp(argv[i], "-input_signal") != 0 ) {
// record the arguments that are not user-defined

npi_argv[npi_argc] = argv[i];
npi_argc++;

}

}
// the argument "-input_signal"
// the next argument is the target string
i++;
input_signal = argv[i]; // record the target string
}

// now you can pass npi_argc and npi_argv to npi_init()
if( !npi_init(npi_argc, npi_argv) )
}

As a result, <verdi import design options> and <NPI options> is saved in npi_argv and the
user-defined option is saved in the "input_signal" variable.

npi_init() and npi_end() : Initialize and Close NPI
npi_init() and npi_end()are used to initialize and end an NPI program. They are required
for all NPI models.
The arguments (npi_argc and npi_argv) passed to npi_init() are call-by-reference,
npi_init() takes the NPI options and only leave the Verdi import design options.

npi_load_design() : Loading Designs in the NPI Program
If you want to use the NPI Language model, the NPI Netlist model, the NPI DM model,
or the NPI Text model, you must call npi_load_design() before using the APIs of those
models.

NPI Options
The following tables list the valid NPI options for npi_init(). If not specified, NPI uses
the default setting.
General Options
-quiet

If specified, the banner, errors and
warnings won't be shown on the console.

Netlist Model Options

Use NPI Model in Tcl

Refer to the NPI Netlist Model chapter for details.

Specify the RTL configurations
<list_of_options>
in the Netlist model.Default is:

"DetailRTL+DetailMux+GenBlock"

| DetailMux | RecogFSM |
GenBlock | RecogLibCell |
RecogMem

Specify the RTL inference level. Default is
100.

<symbol_lib_name>

Specify the symbol library name and path.
Default is NULL.

Use NPI Model in Tcl
* Concept
* Passing Arguments in your NPI Program

Concept
The Verdi executable itself can act as a Tcl interpreter. The Verdi executable can be used
to play any Tcl programs. The usage is similar to the following:
%> verdi -play my_program.tcl <verdi options>

In addition, the Verdi executable includes hundreds of Verdi Tcl commands and the NPI
commands. Therefore, applications can be created by using these commands in your
algorithm. Following is an example of my_program.tcl:
my_program.tcl
puts "Program Name : my_program.tcl"
npi_iterate, npi_scan, npi_get_str, and npi_release_handle are NPI
commands
set top_module_iter [npi_iterate -type npiModule -refHandle ""]
set top_module_hdl [npi_scan -iterator $top_module_iter]
while {$top_module_hdl != ""} { using "" (null string) for NULL handle
set top_module_name [npi_get_str -property "npiName" -object
$top_module_hdl]
puts $top_module_name
npi_release_handle -object $top_module_hdl
set top_module_hdl [npi_scan -iterator $top_module_iter]

Use NPI Model in Tcl

}
following is the Verdi Tcl command that stops the Verdi executable

The program assumes the Verdi executable imports the design first. So playing
my_program.tcl can be executed as follows:
%> verdi -play my_program.tcl -f run.f -path ../Design

"-f run.f -path ../Design" represents the Verdi options for importing the design. Use "verdi
-h" for details. The program lists all the top module names in the design.

Passing Arguments in your NPI Program
Although the Verdi executable can act as a Tcl interpreter, it cannot pass any arguments
from the command line. That is, you cannot use the Tcl command $argv in your
program for the Verdi executable. For example, if you issue the following command
to run the program "my_program2.tcl", Verdi does not parse the argument: "-input
system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode" and thus a runtime error is given.
%> verdi -play my_program2.tcl -f run.f -path ../Design -input
"system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode"

title: Appendix 2274
text:
Verdi cannot parse the argument: "-input system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode". Therefore, if
you wrote the codes below in "my_program2.tcl"

title: Appendix 2274
text:
the following code cannot be accepted by the Verdi executable
set my_arg [lindex $argv 7]

One of the solutions is to use a wrapper Tcl to take in the arguments and then pass them
to the NPI program using environment variables. This is illustrated with the following
example. The tclsh supports the usage of "$argv".
wrap.tcl
!/usr/local/bin/tclsh
set my_arg [lindex $argv 1]
set env(INPUT_SIG) $my_arg
exec verdi -play my_program2.tcl -f run.f
-path ../../demo_gate_design/Design/ &

my_program2.tcl
puts "==============================="
puts "Program Name : my_program2.tcl"

get input argument from the environment variable "INPUT_SIG"
set input_arg $env(INPUT_SIG)
puts "Input : $input_arg"
get the handle of INPUT_SIG, npi_handle_by_name is the NPI command
set hdl [npi_handle_by_name -name $input_arg -scope ""]
set file_name [npi_get_str -property "npiFile" -object $hdl]
set line_no [npi_get -property "npiLineNo" -object $hdl]
puts " File name : $file_name"
puts " Line no. : $line_no"
puts "=============================="
following is the Verdi Tcl command that stops the Verdi executable

Remember to change "wrap.tcl" as executable mode. The program can be run with the
following command. This program outputs the file and line number information for the
specified object in the design.
%> ./wrap.tcl -input "system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode"

The results is similar to the following:
===============================
Program Name : my_program2.tcl
Input : system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode
File name : /demo_gate_design/Design/cpu.vg
Line no. : 604
==============================

The NPI Libraries package is located at the directory $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/L1/C/ in
the Verdi package. It is fine to copy the entire directory to a suitable location and do some
modifications.
If you want to use the default NPI libraries without any customization, NPI provides the
shared library: libnpiL1.so. The following sections describe how to compile and make your
VC Apps executable with libnpiL1.so.
1. In your C/C++ program, include the file "npi_L1.h".
#include "npi_L1.h"

// then your applications can use the APIs in NPI Libraries

The following shows an example that uses the NPI Libraries API,
npi_mod_define_dump_fileName_lineNo, to dump the file name and line number of a
specific module definition.

// header for NPI Models: npi_init,
npi_load_design, npi_end
include "npi_L1.h" // header for NPI Libraries
{
// initialize NPI and load design
// Novas loading design options are contained in argc, argv
// dump file name and line number for the module definition "MOD"
// into the file "output.log"
FILE* pFile = fopen("output.log", "w");
npi_mod_define_dump_fileName_lineNo("MOD", pFile);
fclose(pFile);
// leaving NPI
}

2. Compile and make.
Since NPI Libraries is written using NPI Models, the compile and make steps for NPI
Models are necessary. Refer to Use NPI Models in C/C++ to learn more about how to
compile and make NPI programs.
The following shows the Makefile for the above example "demo.cpp". (Assume the
vg_gnu package is required).
Makefile

title: Appendix 2274
text:
Use NPI Libraries in Tcl
The NPI Libraries package is located at the directory $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/L1/TCL/
in the Verdi package. It is fine to copy the entire directory to a suitable location.
* Install NPI Libraries from the Verdi Package
* Using the NPI Libraries

Install NPI Libraries from the Verdi Package
The NPI Libraries package is located at the directory $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/L1/
TCL/ in the Verdi package. It is fine to copy the entire directory to a suitable location.

Using the NPI Libraries
To use NPI Libraries, you just need to source the file "npi_L1.tcl" at the beginning of your
Tcl program. For example,
source $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/L1/TCL/npi_L1.tcl

then your applications can use the API in NPI Libraries

Setting an environment variable for the path of NPI Libraries is also recommended, for
%> setenv NPIL1_PATH $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/L1/TCL

Then in any of your applications, you just need to source npi_L1.tcl as follows:

then your applications can use the API in NPI Libraries

Use NPI Libraries in Tcl

The following shows an example that uses the NPI Libraries API,
npi_mod_define_dump_fileName_lineNo, to dump the file name and line number of a
specific module definition:
invoke NPI Libraries
dump file name and line number of the module definition "MOD"
into the file "output.log"
set file_handle [open "output.log" "w"]
::npi_L1::npi_mod_define_dump_fileName_lineNo MOD $file_handle
close $file_handle
leaving Novas

Assume the design example.v is as follows:

Then you can use Verdi executable to run the script demo.tcl. (If you are not familiar with
NPI usage, refer to Use NPI Model in Tcl to learn more).
%> verdi -sv example.v -play demo.tcl

"output.log" looks like:
%> cat output.log
%>

The following is an example that uses the NPI Libraries Module library. Assuming a
hierarchical cope is specified by the environment variable "$MOD_SCOPE ", the script
lists all the nets in the scope and check whether a net is used in a continuous assignment.
If so, the corresponding file name and line number is printed.

Use NPI Libraries in Tcl

demo_module_L1.tcl
use NPI Libraries
input : module instance hierarchical name in $env(MOD_SCOPE)
if { [info exists ::env(MOD_SCOPE)] == 0 } {
puts "Please specify the environment variable: \"MOD_SCOPE\""
puts " for the input name of module instance hierarchical"
}
puts "Input module instance = $env(MOD_SCOPE)"
set mod_scope $env(MOD_SCOPE)
get module instance net handle in NPI Libraries Module library
set net_hdl_list {}
set net_num [::npi_L1::npi_mod_inst_get_net $mod_scope net_hdl_list]
iterate all net handle
puts "Net and used continuous assignment:"
for { set i 0 } { [expr $i < $net_num ] } { incr i } {
set net_hdl [lindex $net_hdl_list $i]
puts "$i) [npi_get_str -property npiName -object $net_hdl]"
get the continuous assignment from the net handle
set iter_hdl [npi_iterate -type npiUse -refHandle $net_hdl]
while { [set cont_assign_hdl [npi_scan -iterator $iter_hdl]] != "" } {
if { [npi_get_str -property npiType -object $cont_assign_hdl] ==
"npiContAssign" } {
set fileName [npi_get_str -property npiFile -object $cont_assign_hdl]
set lineNo [npi_get -property npiLineNo -object $cont_assign_hdl]
Continuous assign: $fileName ($lineNo)"
}
}
}
leave Novas

Creating VC Apps by Dynamically Loading Shared Library
The following picture shows the flow of making C/C++ source codes as a shared library
(.so):

Then run the VC Apps by Verdi's Tcl commands (described later) which dynamically loads
the shared library.
In the flow shown in the above figure, you only need the header file of NPI. The following
is unnecessary:
* The libNPI.so and libnpiL1.so.
* The setting of the environment variable $LD_LIBRARY_PATH to the libNPI.so and
libnpL1.so.
* The "npi_init()", "npi_load_design()", and "npi_end()" APIs in the source codes.

Following is an example that demonstrates how to run the VC Apps for the NPI C/C++
program which is compiled as a shared library "my_program.so":
my_program.cpp
#include

<cstdio>
"npi.h" // must have for NPI programs
"npi_hdl.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI Language model
"npi_L1.h" // use NPI L1

// use extern "C" for the shared library loading
extern int my_program_main (int argc, char* argv[]);
}
// do not use the function name "main"; use the function name in the
extern "C" block
// the argument is the same as main()
int my_program_main(int argc, char** argv)
{
// npi_init() is unnecessary
// if( !npi_init(argc, argv) )
// return 0;
// npi_load_design() is unnecessary
// if( !npi_load_design(argc, argv) )
// printf("\n Warning: There are some errors while loading design\n");
printf("\n BEGIN my_program.exe \n");
// the first argument is the top_scope name
string top_scope = argv[1];

CC = g++
CFLAGS = -Wall -fPIC -g
LD = $(CC)
LDFLAGS =
RM = rm

directory setup for NPI include files and shared library (libNPI.so)

VERDI_HOME = /Your_Verdi_Install_Directory
NPI_INC = $(VERDI_HOME)/share/NPI/inc
NPI_L1_INC = $(VERDI_HOME)/share/NPI/L1/C/inc

program setup

EXE = my_program.so
SRCS = my_program.cpp
OBJS = ${SRCS:.cpp=.o}

compiling and linking

.SUFFIXES: .o .cpp
.cpp.o :
$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -I$(NPI_INC) -I$(NPI_L1_INC)
all: $(EXE)
$(EXE): $(NPI_SO) $(OBJS)
$(LD) -shared -o $@ $(OBJS)
@echo "make $(EXE) successful"
clean:

-$(RM) -f $(EXE) $(OBJS)

With the Makefile, it is easy to compile and make my_program.cpp by just typing the
"make" command.
%> make
g++ -Wall -fPIC -g -c my_program.cpp -I/
Your_Verdi_Install_Directory/share/NPI/inc -I/
Your_Verdi_Install_Directory/share/NPI/L1/C/inc
g++ -shared -o my_program.so my_program.o
make my_program.so successful
%>

Loading NPI libraries by the Tcl command - viaSetupL1Apps
Start Verdi executable and import design. Then open the Tcl Command Entry as the
following picture shows:

In the Tcl Command Entry, use "viaSetupL1Apps" command to load the NPI libraries
before loading the shared library. For example:

Dynamically Loading the Shared Library by Verdi - npiDlOpen
In the Tcl Command Entry, use "npiDlOpen" command to load the shared library. For

The description of the Tcl command "npiDlOpen" is as follows:
npiDlOpen -lib <shared library name>
* Description: Open the shared library
* Arguments: -lib <shared_library_name>
Specify the name of the shared library. The relative or absolute path name is allowed.
* Value Returned: 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.

Running the VC Apps in the Shared Library - npiDlSym
In the Tcl Command Entry, use "npiDlOpen" command to run the functions declared in the
extern "C" declaration in the shared library. For example:

The description of the Tcl command "npiDlSym" is as follows:
npiDlSym -func <function name in the shared library> [<argument list>]
* Description: Execute the function in the shared library
* Arguments: -func <function name in the shared library>
Specify the function name declared in the extern "C" block in the shared library.
<argument list>: Specify the argument used in the function specified in -func
option.
* Value Returned: The function returned value. That is, if the function specified in -func
returns 2 during the execution, the Tcl command returns 2 as well.
In the above example, the function name "my_program_main" is used in -func option.
Then the first argument (argv[1]) "test.system.dut.i_cpu" is passed to the function
"my_program_main".
You can pass many arguments to your function. You can also leave the <argument list> as
empty, which means your function doesn't need any arguments.

Use a Tcl Script to Run the VC Apps in the Shared Library
You can use a Tcl script to run the VC Apps of the shared library in the batch mode.
my_program.tcl
puts "Program Name : my_program_main"
npiDlOpen -lib "./my_program.so"
npiDlSym -func "my_program_main" "test.system.dut.i_cpu"
following is the Verdi Tcl command that stops the Verdi executable

The script assumes the Verdi executable imports the design first. So playing
my_program.tcl can be executed as follows:
%> verdi -lib work -top test -play my_program.tcl -batch

The "npi" Utility
In addition to using a Tcl script to run the VC Apps of the shared library, the utility
named "npi" is provided to run in the batch mode. The "npi" utility can be found in
$VERDI_HOME/bin/.
The usage of "npi" utility is as follows:
npi [verdi command options] -dlib <shared library> -dfunc <extern function> -darg
<arguments for the extern function>
* Arguments: [verdi command options]. All Verdi command options.
-dlib <shared library>: The shared library to be loaded by Verdi.
-dfunc <extern function>: The function to be executed by npiDlSym.
-darg <arguments for the extern function>: The arguments for the function
specified by -dfunc.
For example, we can use the "npi" utility to run the function "my_program_main" as
follows:
%> npi -lib work -top test -dlib "./my_program.so" -dfunc
"my_program_main" -darg "test.system.dut.i_cpu"

text:
NPI Language Model
* Quick Start

The NPI Language Model contains models for two languages: SystemVerilog and VHDL.
Users are able to traverse designs from the HDL language perspective. Every construct in
the language is regarded as an object.
For the NPI Language SystemVerilog Model, the IEEE Std 1800 -2009 SystemVerilog
Language Reference Manual (LRM) is applied as the foundation. Most of the
SystemVerilog object model diagrams are similar to the VPI Object Model Diagram in
LRM Chapter 37. For the NPI Language VHDL Model, the IEEE Std1076 -2008 VHDL
Language Reference Manual (LRM) is applied as the foundation. However, the style of the
VHDL object model diagrams follows the NPI Language SystemVerilog Model.
Refer to the API Reference section to see all the APIs that are used in the Language
Model. Refer to the Object Diagram section to understand the HDL language structure and
to learn how to traverse designs through the Language Model.

The following are the APIs available in the NPI Language Model.

The header file (used in C/C++).

npiHandle Data Type
A handle is an opaque reference to an object in the NPI Language Model. It is represented
as a value of the data type npiHandle.
A handle allows an NPI program to refer to an object without assuming details of the
representation of the object. NPI provides functions that operate on objects referred to by
handles.
The particular operations that are legal for an object referred to by a handle depend on the
type of the object.
The following are ways to create or obtain the npiHandle:
1. npi_handle_by_name: Returns a handle that refers to an object identified by a specific
name.
2. npi_handle: Returns a handle that refers to an object in a one-to-one relationship.

3. npi_iterate: Returns a handle to an iterator object for scanning a one-to-many
4. npi_scan: Returns a handle to objects in a one-to-many relationship using their iterator

Obtaining Objects from Design Names: npi_handle_by_name
One of the simplest ways to obtain a npiHandle object is to use npi_handle_by_name.This
function can be applied to all objects with a full name property.
The name can be hierarchical or simple. If scope is NULL (C/C++) or empty string "" (Tcl),
then name is searched for from the top level of hierarchy. If a scope object is provided,
search within that scope.
For example, in the above design example.v, using the following routine in C/C++:
npiHandle module_handle = npi_handle_by_name("TEST.dut", NULL);

or using the following routine in Tcl:
set module_handle [ npi_handle_by_name -name "TEST.dut" -scope "" ]

gets the npiHandle of the module instance object "TEST.dut".

Object Relationships
Each object in a SystemVerilog design is related to other objects. In example.v above, the
module instance "TEST" contains 2 variable objects and the module instance "TEST.dut"
contains three port objects.
In the NPI Language Model, there are two types of object relationships as follows:
1. One-to-one relationships: Occur when an object is only related to another object of a
certain type.
In the example.v, the module instance "TEST.dut" is contained in the module "TEST".
So there is a one-to-one relationship from an instance to its scope.
2. One-to-many relationships: Occur when an object is related to several other objects
of a certain type.
In SystemVerilog HDL, the module might contain more than one net, so there is a oneto-many relationship from the module instance "TEST" to the net objects in example.v.
All the possible relationships that an object might have are documented in the NPI object
diagrams. These object diagrams provide a graphical representation of objects within a
SystemVerilog design to which NPI routines provides access.

The diagrams does not only show the relationships between objects, but also the
properties of each object. Objects with sufficient commonality are placed in a class. Class
relationships and properties apply to all the objects in the class.
The following is a simplified object diagram example:

In this simplified object diagram:
* The solid enclosure designates the objects of type "port".
* The dotted enclosures designate the objects of class "variable" and "scope". The name
of the object class uses an italicized font.
* The double arrow from the "scope" class to the "variable" class indicates a one-to-many
relationship. A "scope" can contain many "variables".
* The single arrow from the "variable" class to the "scope" class indicates a one-to-one
relationship. A specific variable can only occur within one scope.
* There are two single arrows from the "port" object to "variable" class. Above the arrows
are the tags that represent the type of method in the relationship.
The tag "npiHighConn" indicates a one-to-one relationship from the "port" object to
the "variable" class. A specific variable of the port's high connection is obtained.
The tag "npiLowConn" indicates a one-to-one relationship from the "port" object to
the "variable" class. A specific variable of the port's low connection is obtained.
For object relationships, unless a diagram shows a special tag, you can access the type
by adding "npi" to the start of the word inside the enclosure. Capitalize the first letter of
each word.
The following introduces how to traverse the object relationship by NPI routines:
* One-to-one Relationships: npi_handle
* One-to-many Relationships: npi_iterate & npi_scan

One-to-one Relationships: npi_handle
The routine "npi_handle" is used to obtain the objects in a one-to-one relationship. In the
aforementioned figure, the object belonging to the "scope" class can be obtained by:
npiHandle scope_handle = npi_handle (npiScope, variable_handle); // in

or
set scope_handle [ npi_handle -type "npiScope" -refHandle
$variable_handle ]
in Tcl

Similarly, with the "npiHighConn" tag in the single arrow, the one-to-one relationship from a
"port" object to an object belonging to the "variable" class can be obtained by:
npiHandle variable_handle = npi_handle (npiHighConn, port_handle);
// in C/C++

or
set variable_handle [ npi_handle -type "npiHighConn" -refHandle
$port_handle ]
in Tcl

One-to-many Relationships: npi_iterate & npi_scan
The routines "npi_iterate" and "npi_scan" are used to obtain the objects in a one-to-many
The following C/C++ code snippet shows how to use the routines to traverse the "variable"
objects from the object belonging to the "scope" class:
npiHandle iterator = npi_iterate (npiVariable, scope_handle);
npiHandle variable_handle;
while ( (variable_handle = npi_scan(iterator)) != NULL ) {
// do something for the "variable_handle"
}

The following Tcl code snippet shows the routines to traverse the "variable" objects from
the object belonging to the "scope" class:
set iterator [ npi_iterate -type "npiVariable" -refHandle $scope_handle ]
while { [set variable_handle [npi_scan -iterator $iterator]] != "" } {
// do something for the "$variable_handle"
}

Accessing Object Properties: npi_get and npi_get_str
Each object in a SystemVerilog design has some properties. For example, consider the
following simplified object diagram:

In the simplified object diagram, the objects of the class "instance" contain the following
properties:
* Boolean properties: "npiArrayMember", "npiAutomatic", "npiCellInstance", "npiTop".
For Boolean properties, value 1 represents TRUE and value 0 represents FALSE.
* Integer properties: "npiDefLineNo", "npiLineNo", "npiType".
* String properties: "npiDefFile", "npiDefName", "npiFile", "npiName", "npiFullName",
"npiType".
The routine npi_get() is used to obtain a Boolean or integer property of an object. For
example, in C/C++ the property of the instance location "npiLineNo" can be obtained by:
NPI_INT32 line_number = npi_get (npiLineNo, instance_handle);

Or in Tcl the same property can be obtained by:
set line_number [ npi_get -property "npiLineNo" -object
$instance_handle ]

The routine npi_get_str() is used to obtain a string property of an object. For example, in
C/C++ the property of the instance name "npiName" can be obtained by:
NPI_BYTE8* instance_name = npi_get_str (npiName, instance_handle);

Or in Tcl the same property can be obtained by:
set instance_name [ npi_get_str -property "npiName" -object
$instance_handle ]

Other Topics
Handle Release: npi_release_handle
The routine npi_release_handle() called by an NPI program releases a handle. The routine
npi_scan() releases the iterator handle when npi_scan() returns NULL.
It is recommended that an NPI program releases handles when they are no longer
needed.

Lifetimes of Objects
The lifetime of an object is how long it exists in the NPI model. A handle is valid from when
it is created until it is released, the object it points to no longer exists, or the NPI program
ends.
At any other time, the handle is invalid. An NPI program does not use or release an invalid

object that belongs to the class "Nets", in the module instance "TEST.dummy".
end

input clock;
wire clock;
wire [7:0] w1;
wire w2 [0:3]; /* array net */

Remember to include "npi_hdl.h" in the C/C++ program when using the NPI Language

{

NPI Netlist Model
* Introduction to Netlist Object Model
* Special Topics
* Header Files

This model lets users traverse designs from the netlist perspective.
The netlist comes from the Verdi inference database.
You can regard it as technology-independent, non-optimized synthesis results.
In the netlist model, a design has four object types: net, instance, port, and instance port.
Connectivity is provided with the objects.
Refer to the Introduction to Netlist Object Model and Object Diagram sections.
They describe the HDL language structure and how to traverse designs through NPI.
Refer to the API Reference section for Netlist Model APIs.
Refer to the Netlist Model section of Appendix A for the List of All Methods and Properties
and the List of All Supported Methods and Properties for Different Objects.

In the NPI Netlist model, there are four types of objects that are extracted from a design,
instance, port, instance port, and net, as shown in the following figure.

Figure 2

NPI Netlist Object Model

An instance object in the NPI Netlist model is either a module instance or a primitive
instance. A module instance denotes a module reference in the design that serves as a
container for sub instance, port, instance port, and net objects.
A primitive instance denotes the minimum design unit. It is used to represent low-level
logic gates and switches with specific cell functions.
For example, npiNlAndCell, npiNlFSMCell, and npiNlBufCell. The following figure is a
simple example showing the concept of module instance and primitive instance objects in
the NPI Netlist model:
Figure 3

Instance Objects in NPI Netlist Model

For detailed information about properties and relationships of an instance object, refer to
the Instance Ports object diagram.
A port object represents a port of a module instance. It is used to connect instance port
and net objects belonging to the module instance.
For detailed information about properties and relationships of port objects, refer to the Text
Model object diagram.

Instance Port
An instance port object represents the port instance along with the instance object. In
the NPI Netlist model, each instance port object has a specific property to indicate its
functional type.
For example, npiNlDataPort, npiNlClockPort, and npiNlLatchedPort. For detailed
information about properties and relationships of instance port objects, refer to the
Instance Ports object diagram.
Net
A net object represents physical connections between structural entities, such as instance
port and port.
For detailed information about properties and relationships of net objects, refer to the Text
Model object diagram.
The following shows the source code of the RTL design CPUsystem.
module CPUsystem (RESET, CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4);
input CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4;
input RESET;
wire [7:0] addr, data,
wire VMA, R_W, BUSY;
wire [7:0] RAM20, RAM21, RAM22, RAM23,
wire [7:0] PC, IXR;
wire IR_load;
CPU i_CPU (CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4, RESET
VMA, R_W ,BUSY, data, addr);
pram i_pram (CLOCK1, VMA, R_W, BUSY, addr, data);

In this HDL code, the top module CPUsystem contains several module instantiations and
wire declarations.
In the resulting NPI Netlist model (see the following figure), CPUsustem is modeled as a
module instance object that contains:
* Two instance objects, i_CPU and i_pram.
* Five port objects, CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4, and RESET.

* Ten net objects, BUSY, CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4, RESET, R W, VMA,
addr[7:0], and data[7:0].
Figure 4

NPI Netlist Model of the RTL Design

The NPI Netlist model depends on the Verdi inference engine and might discard useless

Pseudo Object
As mentioned before, the NPI Netlist model contains different objects. Such objects are
called actual objects.
For an actual object, you can perform object-level traversing through the APIs (see Object
Diagram and API Reference).
To make it easier for bit-level traversing, the NPI Netlist model creates a different type of
object, called pseudo object.
A pseudo object is dynamically created from an actual object based on the bit range given
for traversing.

In the NPI Netlist model, an actual object is regarded as the parent of the created
pseudo objects. Actually, a pseudo object is equivalent to its parent object on object-level
traversing, but it only covers a specific sub range of its parent object.
The purpose of the pseudo object is mainly for easier bit-level traversing.

NPI Netlist Handles
A handle is an opaque reference to an object in the NPI Netlist model. It is represented as
a value of the data type npiNlHandle.
However, the interpretation of the representation is implementation defined. A handle
allows an NPI Netlist program to refer to an object without assuming details of the
representation of the object.
The NPI Netlist provides functions that operate on objects referred to by handles.
The particular operations that are legal for an object referred to by a handle depend on the
type of the object.
* Handle Creation
* Handle Release
* Validity of Handles

Handle Creation
A handle might be created by one of the following functions in an NPI Netlist application
program:
1. npi_nl_handle: Returns a handle that refers to an object in a one-to-one relationship.
2. npi_nl_handle_by_index: Returns a handle to an object based on the index number of
the object within the reference object.

3. npi_nl_handle_by_range: Returns a handle to an object based on the specified range
of the object within the reference object.
4. npi_nl_handle_by_name: Returns a handle that refers to an object identified by a
specific name.
5. npi_nl_iterate: Returns a handle to an iterator object for scanning a one-to-many
6. npi_nl_iterate_with_range: Returns a handle to an iterator object for scanning a one-tomany relationship under the given range.
7. npi_nl_scan: Returns a handle to objects in a one-to-many relationship, using their
iterator object.
The number of handles that an implementation can create might be
constrained by the capacity of the host system.

Handle Release
The function npi_nl_release_handle called by an NPI Netlist program causes a tool to
release a handle.
If a tool shares resources associated with handles and one NPI Netlist program releases a
handle, other NPI Netlist programs is able to continue to refer to objects using handles that
they have not released.
The tool might reclaim resources associated with the representation of a released handle.
* It is recommended that an NPI Netlist program release handles when they
are no longer needed.
* A tool might reclaim resources associated with a handle when the handle
is released by an NPI Netlist program, provided the requirements of Handle
Creation are met.
As a consequence, resources might not be reclaimed immediately upon
release of a handle by an NPI Netlist program, as the resources might be
associated with handles in use by other NPI Netlist programs.

Validity of Handles
A handle is said to be valid from the time of its creation until the time it is released, or until
the object that it refers to ceases to exist, or until termination of the tool; at other times it is
invalid.

A NPI Netlist program does not refer to an object using an invalid handle, nor is an NPI
Netlist program attempt to release an invalid handle.

NPI Netlist Object Classifications
NPI Netlist objects are classified using object diagrams. These diagrams provide a
graphical representation of those objects within a Netlist model to which the NPI Netlist
routines provides access.
The diagrams show the relationships between objects and the properties of each object.
Objects with sufficient commonality are placed in groups. Group relationships and
properties apply to all objects in the group.
As an example, the simplified diagram in Figure 1 shows that there is a one-to-many
relationship from objects of type inst to objects of type port and a one-to-one relationship
from objects of type port to objects of type inst.
Objects of type port have properties npiNlName, and npiNlSize with data types string and
integer, respectively.

Examples of Object Relationships Diagram

For object relationships (unless a special tag is shown in the diagram), the type used for
access is determined by adding "npiNl" to the beginning of the word within the enclosure
and capitalizing each word's first letter.
Using the above example, if an application has a handle to a port and wants to go to the
instance where the port is defined, the call would be as follows:
instH = npi_nl_handle(npiNlInst, portH);

where portH is a handle to the port. As another example, to access an "instport" object,
use the type "npiNlInstPort".

Accessing Object Relationships and Properties
The NPI Netlist defines the C data type of npiNlHandle. All objects are manipulated
through a npiNlHandle variable.
Object handles can be accessed from a relationship with another object or from a
hierarchical name as the following example demonstrates:
npiNlHandle net;
net = npi_nl_handle_by_name("top.m1.w1");

This example call retrieves a handle to wire top.m1.w1 and assigns it to the npiNlHandle
variable, net.
The NPI Netlist provides generic functions, such as traversing relationships and
determining property values.
One-to-one relationships are traversed with the function npi_nl_handle. In the following
example, the instance that contains net is derived from a handle to that net:
npiNlHandle net, inst;
net = npi_nl_handle_by_name("top.m1.w1");
inst = npi_nl_handle(npiNlInst, net);

The call to npi_nl_handle in the above example returns a handle to instance top.m1.
Sometimes it is necessary to access a class of objects that do not have a name or whose
name is ambiguous with another class of objects that can be accessed from the reference
Tags are used in this situation, as shown in Figure 2.
Figure 22

Accessing a Class of Objects Using Tags

In this example, the tag npiNlParent is used instead of npiNlPort to access the actual port
of the pseudo port object.
Properties of objects can be accessed by routines in the npi_nl_get family. The routine
npi_nl_get returns integer and Boolean properties.
Integer and Boolean properties are defined to be of type NPI_INT32. For Boolean
properties, a value of 1 represents TRUE and a value of 0 represents FALSE.
The routine npi_nl_get_str accesses string properties. String properties are defined to be
of type NPI_BYTE8 *.

For example, to retrieve a pointer to the full hierarchical name of the object referenced by
handle inst, the following call would be made:
const NPI_BYTE8 *name = npi_nl_get_str(npiNlFullName, inst);

In the above example, the pointer "name" points to the string "top.m1".
One-to-many relationships are traversed by an iteration mechanism. The routine
npi_nl_iterate (or npi_nl_iterate_with_range) creates an object of type npiNlIterator, which
is then passed to the routine npi_nl_scan to traverse the desired objects.
In the following example, each net in instance top.m1 is displayed:
npiNlHandle net, itr;
itr = npi_nl_iterate(npiNlNet, inst);
while ( net = npi_nl_scan(itr) )
printf("\t%s\n", npi_nl_get_str(npiNlFullName, net));

As the above example illustrates, the naming convention for function is `npi_nl' prefix with
`_' word as delimiter (for example, npi_nl_get_str).
On the other hand, macro defined types and properties are named by `npiNl' prefix with
capitalization for each word (for example, npiNlFullName).
The routines for traversing Netlist model and accessing objects are described in the API
Referencesection.

Object Type Properties
All objects have a npiNlType property

npi_nl_get(npiNlType, <object handle>)returns an integer constant that represents the type
of the object.
npi_nl_get_str(npiNlType, <object handle>) returns a pointer to a string containing the
name of the type constant.
The name of the type constant is derived from the name of the object shown in the object
diagram (see NPI Netlist Object Classifications for a description of how type constant
names are derived from object names).
All objects except iterators have a npiNlLangType property.

The npiNlLangType property returns the language type of the object, that is, the object is
inferred from which language model.

Available values include npiNlSystemVerilog and npiNlVHDL. Similar to the npiNlType
property, npiNlLangType can be accessed using npi_nl_get and npi_nl_get_str.
Some objects have other types of properties npiNlInstType, npiNlCellType, and
npiNlPortType. npi_nl_get(<type property>, <object handle>) returns an integer constant
that represents these properties.
See npi_nl.h for the types that can be returned for these properties. The constant names
of these properties can be accessed using npi_nl_get_str.
In addition to the above type properties, properties npiNlDirection and npiNlPortState can
also be accessed using both npi_nl_get and npi_nl_get_str.
For detailed information of available values of these properties, refer to npi_nl.h.

Object Name Properties
All objects except iterators have npiNlName and npiNlFullName properties.

The npiNlName property returns the name of the object, and the npiNlFullName property
returns the full hierarchical name of the object.
In the NPI Netlist model, the names of pseudo objects contain additional strings for
representing the range information.
The naming convention is a `#' prefix with [<left>:<right>], where<left> and <right> denote
the range of the pseudo object.
For example, a pseudo net object represents as part-select [2:1] of a net object named
"a[3:0]", the npiNlName property of the pseudo net object returns "a[3:0]#[2:1]".

An always process object. Within the process is a named begin scope object with
the name "B1". Within the named begin scope is the if-else statement object.

npiHandle Data Type
A handle is an opaque reference to an object in the NPI Language Model. It is represented
as a value of the data type npiHandle.
A handle allows an NPI program to refer to an object without assuming details of the
representation of the object. NPI provides functions that operate on objects referred to by
handles.
The particular operations that are legal for an object referred to by a handle depend on the
type of the object.
The following are ways to create or obtain the npiHandle:
1. npi_handle_by_name: Returns a handle that refers to an object identified by a specific
name.
2. npi_handle: Returns a handle that refers to an object in a one-to-one relationship.

3. npi_iterate: Returns a handle to an iterator object for scanning a one-to-many
4. npi_scan: Returns a handle to objects in a one-to-many relationship using their iterator

Obtaining Objects from Design Names: npi_handle_by_name
One of the simplest ways to obtain a npiHandle object is to use npi_handle_by_name.This
function can be applied to all objects with a full name property.
The name can be hierarchical or simple. If scope is NULL (C/C++) or empty string "" (Tcl),
then name is searched for from the top level of hierarchy. If a scope object is provided,
search within that scope.
For example, in the above design example.v, using the following routine in C/C++:
npiHandle module_handle = npi_handle_by_name("TEST.dut", NULL);

or using the following routine in Tcl:
set module_handle [ npi_handle_by_name -name "TEST.dut" -scope "" ]

gets the npiHandle of the module instance object "TEST.dut".

Object Relationships
Each object in a SystemVerilog design is related to other objects. In example.v above, the
module instance "TEST" contains 2 variable objects and the module instance "TEST.dut"
contains three port objects.
In the NPI Language Model, there are two types of object relationships as follows:
1. One-to-one relationships: Occur when an object is only related to another object of a
certain type.
In the example.v, the module instance "TEST.dut" is contained in the module "TEST".
So there is a one-to-one relationship from an instance to its scope.
2. One-to-many relationships: Occur when an object is related to several other objects
of a certain type.
In SystemVerilog HDL, the module might contain more than one net, so there is a oneto-many relationship from the module instance "TEST" to the net objects in example.v.
All the possible relationships that an object might have are documented in the NPI object
diagrams. These object diagrams provide a graphical representation of objects within a
SystemVerilog design to which NPI routines provides access.

The diagrams does not only show the relationships between objects, but also the
properties of each object. Objects with sufficient commonality are placed in a class. Class
relationships and properties apply to all the objects in the class.
The following is a simplified object diagram example:

In this simplified object diagram:
* The solid enclosure designates the objects of type "port".
* The dotted enclosures designate the objects of class "variable" and "scope". The name
of the object class uses an italicized font.
* The double arrow from the "scope" class to the "variable" class indicates a one-to-many
relationship. A "scope" can contain many "variables".
* The single arrow from the "variable" class to the "scope" class indicates a one-to-one
relationship. A specific variable can only occur within one scope.
* There are two single arrows from the "port" object to "variable" class. Above the arrows
are the tags that represent the type of method in the relationship.
The tag "npiHighConn" indicates a one-to-one relationship from the "port" object to
the "variable" class. A specific variable of the port's high connection is obtained.
The tag "npiLowConn" indicates a one-to-one relationship from the "port" object to
the "variable" class. A specific variable of the port's low connection is obtained.
For object relationships, unless a diagram shows a special tag, you can access the type
by adding "npi" to the start of the word inside the enclosure. Capitalize the first letter of
each word.
The following introduces how to traverse the object relationship by NPI routines:
* One-to-one Relationships: npi_handle
* One-to-many Relationships: npi_iterate & npi_scan

One-to-one Relationships: npi_handle
The routine "npi_handle" is used to obtain the objects in a one-to-one relationship. In the
aforementioned figure, the object belonging to the "scope" class can be obtained by:
npiHandle scope_handle = npi_handle (npiScope, variable_handle); // in

or
set scope_handle [ npi_handle -type "npiScope" -refHandle
$variable_handle ]
in Tcl

Similarly, with the "npiHighConn" tag in the single arrow, the one-to-one relationship from a
"port" object to an object belonging to the "variable" class can be obtained by:
npiHandle variable_handle = npi_handle (npiHighConn, port_handle);
// in C/C++

or
set variable_handle [ npi_handle -type "npiHighConn" -refHandle
$port_handle ]
in Tcl

One-to-many Relationships: npi_iterate & npi_scan
The routines "npi_iterate" and "npi_scan" are used to obtain the objects in a one-to-many
The following C/C++ code snippet shows how to use the routines to traverse the "variable"
objects from the object belonging to the "scope" class:
npiHandle iterator = npi_iterate (npiVariable, scope_handle);
npiHandle variable_handle;
while ( (variable_handle = npi_scan(iterator)) != NULL ) {
// do something for the "variable_handle"
}

The following Tcl code snippet shows the routines to traverse the "variable" objects from
the object belonging to the "scope" class:
set iterator [ npi_iterate -type "npiVariable" -refHandle $scope_handle ]
while { [set variable_handle [npi_scan -iterator $iterator]] != "" } {

Tcl Example
load the design
debImport -sv design.v
set dummy_inst_hdl [ npi_handle_by_name -name "TEST.dummy" -scope "" ]
puts "Module= [npi_get_str -property npiFullName -object
$dummy_inst_hdl]"
traverse net
set net_itr [ npi_iterate -type npiNet -refHandle $dummy_inst_hdl ]
while { [set net_hdl [npi_scan -iterator $net_itr]] != "" } {
puts " Net= \t [npi_get_str -property npiName -object $net_hdl] \t
([npi_get_str -property npiNetType -object $net_hdl])"
}
traverse array net
set net_itr [ npi_iterate -type npiArrayNet -refHandle $dummy_inst_hdl ]
while { [set net_hdl [npi_scan -iterator $net_itr]] != "" } {
puts " Array Net= \t [npi_get_str -property npiName -object $net_hdl] \t
([npi_get_str -property npiNetType -object $net_hdl])"
}
exit novas

Refer to the npi_hdl.h section in Appendix C for the npi_hdl.h header file details.

NPI Netlist Model
* Introduction to Netlist Object Model
* Special Topics
* Header Files

This model lets users traverse designs from the netlist perspective.
The netlist comes from the Verdi inference database.
You can regard it as technology-independent, non-optimized synthesis results.
In the netlist model, a design has four object types: net, instance, port, and instance port.
Connectivity is provided with the objects.
Refer to the Introduction to Netlist Object Model and Object Diagram sections.
They describe the HDL language structure and how to traverse designs through NPI.
Refer to the API Reference section for Netlist Model APIs.
Refer to the Netlist Model section of Appendix A for the List of All Methods and Properties
and the List of All Supported Methods and Properties for Different Objects.

In the NPI Netlist model, there are four types of objects that are extracted from a design,
instance, port, instance port, and net, as shown in the following figure.

Figure 2

NPI Netlist Object Model

An instance object in the NPI Netlist model is either a module instance or a primitive
instance. A module instance denotes a module reference in the design that serves as a
container for sub instance, port, instance port, and net objects.
A primitive instance denotes the minimum design unit. It is used to represent low-level
logic gates and switches with specific cell functions.
For example, npiNlAndCell, npiNlFSMCell, and npiNlBufCell. The following figure is a
simple example showing the concept of module instance and primitive instance objects in
the NPI Netlist model:
Figure 3

Instance Objects in NPI Netlist Model

For detailed information about properties and relationships of an instance object, refer to
the Instance Ports object diagram.
A port object represents a port of a module instance. It is used to connect instance port
and net objects belonging to the module instance.
For detailed information about properties and relationships of port objects, refer to the Text
Model object diagram.

Instance Port
An instance port object represents the port instance along with the instance object. In
the NPI Netlist model, each instance port object has a specific property to indicate its
functional type.
For example, npiNlDataPort, npiNlClockPort, and npiNlLatchedPort. For detailed
information about properties and relationships of instance port objects, refer to the
Instance Ports object diagram.
Net
A net object represents physical connections between structural entities, such as instance
port and port.
For detailed information about properties and relationships of net objects, refer to the Text
Model object diagram.
The following shows the source code of the RTL design CPUsystem.
module CPUsystem (RESET, CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4);
input CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4;
input RESET;
wire [7:0] addr, data,
wire VMA, R_W, BUSY;
wire [7:0] RAM20, RAM21, RAM22, RAM23,
wire [7:0] PC, IXR;
wire IR_load;
CPU i_CPU (CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4, RESET
VMA, R_W ,BUSY, data, addr);
pram i_pram (CLOCK1, VMA, R_W, BUSY, addr, data);

In this HDL code, the top module CPUsystem contains several module instantiations and
wire declarations.
In the resulting NPI Netlist model (see the following figure), CPUsustem is modeled as a
module instance object that contains:
* Two instance objects, i_CPU and i_pram.
* Five port objects, CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4, and RESET.

* Ten net objects, BUSY, CLOCK1, CLOCK2, CLOCK3, CLOCK4, RESET, R W, VMA,
addr[7:0], and data[7:0].
Figure 4

NPI Netlist Model of the RTL Design

The NPI Netlist model depends on the Verdi inference engine and might discard useless
wires or registers.
For example, in the code and above figure, wires RAM20, RAM21, RAM22, RAM23, PC,
IXR, IR_load are floating nets in the design and do not end up in the NPI Netlist model.

Pseudo Object
As mentioned before, the NPI Netlist model contains different objects. Such objects are
called actual objects.
For an actual object, you can perform object-level traversing through the APIs (see Object
Diagram and API Reference).
To make it easier for bit-level traversing, the NPI Netlist model creates a different type of
object, called pseudo object.
A pseudo object is dynamically created from an actual object based on the bit range given
for traversing.

In the NPI Netlist model, an actual object is regarded as the parent of the created
pseudo objects. Actually, a pseudo object is equivalent to its parent object on object-level
traversing, but it only covers a specific sub range of its parent object.
The purpose of the pseudo object is mainly for easier bit-level traversing.
The Figure 5 figure shows an example of an actual object connection. In this case,
"p_in[3:0]" is an instance port object, and "a[1:0],b[1:0]", "a[1:0]", "b[1:0]", "a[0]", and "a[1]"
are net objects with different types.
The actual object connectivity relationships are listed as follows:
"p_in[3:0]"

to

"a[1:0],b[1:0]"

"a[1:0],b[1:0]"

to

"p_in[3:0]", "a[1:0]", and "b[1:0]"

"a[1:0]"

to

"a[1:0],b[1:0]", "a[0]", and "a[1]"

"b[1:0]"

to

"a[1:0],b[1:0]"

"a[1]"

to

"a[1:0]"

"a[0]"

to

"a[1:0]"

Figure 5

Connectivity Relationships between Actual Objects

The object-level connectivity relationship can also be presented as bus connections as
shown in the following figure:
Figure 6

Object-level Connectivity Relationships between Actual Objects

In bit-level traversing, the connectivity relationship of net object "a[1]" should be the most
significant bit of net object "a[1:0]" instead of the full bus of "a[1:0]".
To present such an object, the NPI Netlist creates a net object called "a[1:0]#[1]", which is
a pseudo object dynamically created from the actual object "a[1:0]".

Schematic Configurations
The NPI Netlist can operate with different schematic configurations. In this sub clause,
these configurations together with examples are described.

RTL Configurations
The following are the list of RTL configurations:
* DetailRTL: If the option is set, instances is inferred in detailed view.
* DetailLevel: Use this option to control the Netlist RTL level. The input value takes
effect only when the DetailRTL option is on.
The level number must be a positive number. Otherwise, the default value 4 is applied.
The following figures are an example of DetailRTL with different level configurations:
wire a, b, c, d;
assign d = (a || b) && c;

Figure 8

DetailRTL= "off"

Figure 9

DetailRTL= "on", DetailLevel=1

Figure 10

DetailRTL= "on", DetailLevel=2

* DetailMux: If this option is set, unintended latches are extracted as MUX style in the
detailed schematics.

The input value takes effect only when the DetailRTL option is on. The
following figures are examples of a DetailMux configuration:
module mux;
wire [1:0] sel;
reg q, a1, a2, a3;
always @(sel)
case (sel)
2'b00: q = a1;
2'b01: q = a2;
2'b10: q = a3;

Figure 11

DetailRTL= "on", DetailMux= "off"

Figure 12

DetailRTL= "on", DetailMux= "on"

* RecogFSM: If this option is set, FSM recognition applies to the inferred objects. The
following figures are examples of RecogFSM configuration.
reg [1:0] CurrStateFSM3, NextStateFSM3;
wire Clock;
parameter ST_Sum1 = 0, ST_Sum2 = 1, ST_Sum3 = 2,
ST_NoSum = 3;
always @(CurrStateFSM3) begin
case (CurrStateFSM3)
ST_Sum1: NextStateFSM3 = ST_Sum2;
ST_Sum2: NextStateFSM3 = ST_Sum3;
ST_Sum3: NextStateFSM3 = ST_Sum1;
ST_NoSum: NextStateFSM3 = ST_Sum1;
default: NextStateFSM3 = ST_Sum1;
end
always @(posedge Clock) begin
CurrStateFSM3 = NextStateFSM3;
end

Figure 13

RecogFSM= "off"

Figure 14

RecogFSM= "on"

* GenBlock: If this option is set, when the GENERATE block is at the architecture level,
the block is expanded and individual instances are inferred. If the If the block is at the
RTL level, this option has no effect.
The following figure is an example of GenBlock configuration.
wire [2:0] a, b, c;
for (i=0;i<=2;i=i+1) begin
assign a[i]= b[i]&&c[i];
end

Figure 15

GenBlock= "off"

Figure 16

GenBlock= "on"

* RecogLibCell / InferenceLibCell: When symbol libraries do not exist, cells defined
with `celldefine or `endcelledefine, or cells imported with the -v or -y options are
recognized as modules if this option is set.
It should be noted that the global settings are applied after turning on this option, and
all the tracing results are reset. The following figure is an example of RecogLibCell
configuration.
wire z, a, b;
AN2 an2(z, a, b);
celldefine
module AN2(Z, A, B);
input A, B;
output Z;
and 1 ( Z, A, B);
endcelldefine

Figure 17

RecogLibCell = "off"

Figure 18

RecogLibCell = "on"

* RecogMem:If this option is set, when the MEMORY block is at the architecture level,
the block would be expanded and individual instances are inferred.
If the block is at the RTL level, this option does not have an effect. The following figure
is an example of RecogMem configuration.
typedef logic [7:0] ubyte;
clock;
logic
VMA;
logic
R_W;
ubyte
addr;
wire [7:0] data;
ubyte
macroram [255:0];
ubyte
dataout;
assign data = R_W ? dataout : 8'hz;
always @(posedge (clock & VMA))
if (R_W == 1) dataout=macroram[addr];
else macroram[addr]=data;
end

Figure 19

RecogMem = "off"

Figure 20

RecogMem = "on"

* RegName: The option specifies the naming rule for the inferred registers. If the option
is set, the inferred register names have the following format:
<full hierarchy scope>.<register naming rule><output signal name of register
instance>#<internal code name>
The option affects the register names if the option DetailRTL is "on".
The delimiter is user-defined and subject to change.

Symbol Library Configurations
Symbol Library Names: The option specifies the preferred symbol library names in
this text field. Multiple library names can be separated by either a space or a colon (:)
character.
Symbol Library Paths: The option specifies the preferred symbol library paths in this text
field. Multiple path strings can be separated by either a space or a colon (:) character.

The following list of APIs are available in all NPI models:

npi.h

The header for all NPI applications (used in C/C++)

NPI Netlist Handles
A handle is an opaque reference to an object in the NPI Netlist model. It is represented as
a value of the data type npiNlHandle.
However, the interpretation of the representation is implementation defined. A handle
allows an NPI Netlist program to refer to an object without assuming details of the
representation of the object.
The NPI Netlist provides functions that operate on objects referred to by handles.
The particular operations that are legal for an object referred to by a handle depend on the
type of the object.
* Handle Creation
* Handle Release
* Validity of Handles

Handle Creation
A handle might be created by one of the following functions in an NPI Netlist application
program:
1. npi_nl_handle: Returns a handle that refers to an object in a one-to-one relationship.
2. npi_nl_handle_by_index: Returns a handle to an object based on the index number of
the object within the reference object.

3. npi_nl_handle_by_range: Returns a handle to an object based on the specified range
of the object within the reference object.
4. npi_nl_handle_by_name: Returns a handle that refers to an object identified by a
specific name.
5. npi_nl_iterate: Returns a handle to an iterator object for scanning a one-to-many
6. npi_nl_iterate_with_range: Returns a handle to an iterator object for scanning a one-tomany relationship under the given range.
7. npi_nl_scan: Returns a handle to objects in a one-to-many relationship, using their
iterator object.
The number of handles that an implementation can create might be
constrained by the capacity of the host system.

Handle Release
The function npi_nl_release_handle called by an NPI Netlist program causes a tool to
release a handle.
If a tool shares resources associated with handles and one NPI Netlist program releases a
handle, other NPI Netlist programs is able to continue to refer to objects using handles that
they have not released.
The tool might reclaim resources associated with the representation of a released handle.
* It is recommended that an NPI Netlist program release handles when they
are no longer needed.
* A tool might reclaim resources associated with a handle when the handle
is released by an NPI Netlist program, provided the requirements of Handle
Creation are met.
As a consequence, resources might not be reclaimed immediately upon
release of a handle by an NPI Netlist program, as the resources might be
associated with handles in use by other NPI Netlist programs.

Validity of Handles
A handle is said to be valid from the time of its creation until the time it is released, or until
the object that it refers to ceases to exist, or until termination of the tool; at other times it is
invalid.

A NPI Netlist program does not refer to an object using an invalid handle, nor is an NPI
Netlist program attempt to release an invalid handle.

NPI Netlist Object Classifications
NPI Netlist objects are classified using object diagrams. These diagrams provide a
graphical representation of those objects within a Netlist model to which the NPI Netlist
routines provides access.
The diagrams show the relationships between objects and the properties of each object.
Objects with sufficient commonality are placed in groups. Group relationships and
properties apply to all objects in the group.
As an example, the simplified diagram in Figure 1 shows that there is a one-to-many
relationship from objects of type inst to objects of type port and a one-to-one relationship
from objects of type port to objects of type inst.
Objects of type port have properties npiNlName, and npiNlSize with data types string and
integer, respectively.

access is determined by adding "npiNl" to the beginning of the word within the enclosure
and capitalizing each word's first letter.
Using the above example, if an application has a handle to a port and wants to go to the
instance where the port is defined, the call would be as follows:
instH = npi_nl_handle(npiNlInst, portH);

where portH is a handle to the port. As another example, to access an "instport" object,
use the type "npiNlInstPort".
* Accessing Object Relationships and Properties

Accessing Object Relationships and Properties
The NPI Netlist defines the C data type of npiNlHandle. All objects are manipulated
through a npiNlHandle variable.
Object handles can be accessed from a relationship with another object or from a
hierarchical name as the following example demonstrates:
npiNlHandle net;
net = npi_nl_handle_by_name("top.m1.w1");

This example call retrieves a handle to wire top.m1.w1 and assigns it to the npiNlHandle
variable, net.
The NPI Netlist provides generic functions, such as traversing relationships and
determining property values.
One-to-one relationships are traversed with the function npi_nl_handle. In the following
example, the instance that contains net is derived from a handle to that net:
npiNlHandle net, inst;
net = npi_nl_handle_by_name("top.m1.w1");
inst = npi_nl_handle(npiNlInst, net);

The call to npi_nl_handle in the above example returns a handle to instance top.m1.
Sometimes it is necessary to access a class of objects that do not have a name or whose
name is ambiguous with another class of objects that can be accessed from the reference
Tags are used in this situation, as shown in Figure 2.
Figure 22

Accessing a Class of Objects Using Tags

In this example, the tag npiNlParent is used instead of npiNlPort to access the actual port
of the pseudo port object.
Properties of objects can be accessed by routines in the npi_nl_get family. The routine
npi_nl_get returns integer and Boolean properties.
Integer and Boolean properties are defined to be of type NPI_INT32. For Boolean
properties, a value of 1 represents TRUE and a value of 0 represents FALSE.
The routine npi_nl_get_str accesses string properties. String properties are defined to be
of type NPI_BYTE8 *.

In the above example, the pointer "name" points to the string "top.m1".
One-to-many relationships are traversed by an iteration mechanism. The routine
npi_nl_iterate (or npi_nl_iterate_with_range) creates an object of type npiNlIterator, which
is then passed to the routine npi_nl_scan to traverse the desired objects.
In the following example, each net in instance top.m1 is displayed:
npiNlHandle net, itr;
itr = npi_nl_iterate(npiNlNet, inst);
while ( net = npi_nl_scan(itr) )
printf("\t%s\n", npi_nl_get_str(npiNlFullName, net));

As the above example illustrates, the naming convention for function is `npi_nl' prefix with
`_' word as delimiter (for example, npi_nl_get_str).
On the other hand, macro defined types and properties are named by `npiNl' prefix with
capitalization for each word (for example, npiNlFullName).
The routines for traversing Netlist model and accessing objects are described in the API
Referencesection.

Object Type Properties
All objects have a npiNlType property

npi_nl_get(npiNlType, <object handle>)returns an integer constant that represents the type
of the object.
npi_nl_get_str(npiNlType, <object handle>) returns a pointer to a string containing the
name of the type constant.
The name of the type constant is derived from the name of the object shown in the object
diagram (see NPI Netlist Object Classifications for a description of how type constant
names are derived from object names).
All objects except iterators have a npiNlLangType property.

The npiNlLangType property returns the language type of the object, that is, the object is
inferred from which language model.

Available values include npiNlSystemVerilog and npiNlVHDL. Similar to the npiNlType
property, npiNlLangType can be accessed using npi_nl_get and npi_nl_get_str.
Some objects have other types of properties npiNlInstType, npiNlCellType, and
npiNlPortType. npi_nl_get(<type property>, <object handle>) returns an integer constant
that represents these properties.
See npi_nl.h for the types that can be returned for these properties. The constant names
of these properties can be accessed using npi_nl_get_str.
In addition to the above type properties, properties npiNlDirection and npiNlPortState can
also be accessed using both npi_nl_get and npi_nl_get_str.
For detailed information of available values of these properties, refer to npi_nl.h.

Object Name Properties
All objects except iterators have npiNlName and npiNlFullName properties.

The npiNlName property returns the name of the object, and the npiNlFullName property
returns the full hierarchical name of the object.
In the NPI Netlist model, the names of pseudo objects contain additional strings for
representing the range information.
The naming convention is a `#' prefix with [<left>:<right>], where<left> and <right> denote
the range of the pseudo object.
For example, a pseudo net object represents as part-select [2:1] of a net object named
"a[3:0]", the npiNlName property of the pseudo net object returns "a[3:0]#[2:1]".

NPI Text Model

* Support and Limitations

The NPI Text Model lets the user traverse or manipulate design source codes from a
text perspective. Every file, line and word is regarded as an object and the traversing
and manipulative APIs are provided. In addition to the basic insert, delete, and replace
capabilities, you can access the attribute of each word from the design analysis results of
the Verdi system.
Refer to the API Reference for all the APIs provided in the Text model. To understand
the types of all supported NPI Text objects and how to traverse Text objects, refer to the
Object Diagram. The details for the word attribute can be found in Appendix B: Text Word
Attribute (TWA) Types.

The following are the APIs available in the NPI Text Model.

An NPI Text handle is an opaque reference to an object in the Text model. The Text model
provides APIs to traverse or manipulate objects through these handles.
The NPI Text model contains two types of handles. One is npiTextHandle, which
represents a handle referring to a Text object. The other is npiTextIter, which represents a
handle referring to an iterator that iterates npiTextHandle.
Text model objects are presented in the style of the VPI data model diagrams as in chapter

Using NPI Text Model in Tcl Programming
In this section, a sample showing you how to work with the NPI Text model Tcl interface is
introduced. The sample Tcl script traverses word attributes of all design files.
The design file is "example.v":

The Tcl program is "word_attribute.tcl":
set file_iter [ npi_text_iter_start -type "npiTextFile" -ref "" ]
while { "" != [ set file_hdl [ npi_text_iter_next -iter $file_iter ] ] }
{
set file_name [ npi_text_property_str -type "npiTextFileName" -ref
puts "file name : $file_name"
while { "" != [ set line_hdl [ npi_text_iter_next -iter $line_iter ] ] }
{
set line_content [ npi_text_property_str -type "npiTextLineContent" -ref
puts "line_content:"
puts -nonewline $line_content
while { ""!= [ set word_hdl [ npi_text_iter_next -iter $word_iter ] ] } {
puts -nonewline [ npi_text_property_str -type "npiTextWordName" -ref
$word_hdl ]
set word_attribute [ npi_text_property_str -type "npiTextWordAttribute"
-ref
$word_hdl ]
puts -nonewline "($word_attribute)"
}
}

}
npi_text_iter_stop -iter $file_iter

The following command can be used to execute the script:
%> novas example.v -play word_attribute.tcl

NPI Design Manipulation (DM) Model
The functions associated with the Design Manipulation Model are still
considered beta quality.

NPI DM model lets users traverse designs from a module-based perspective and also lets
users manipulate their design. Module-based design traversal means the traversal scope
is in the module definition, not in the module instance that contains the after-elaboration
results. Traversing and manipulating module definitions works similar to editing HDL code
by a hardware designer. Adding or deleting a port in a module definition impacts all the
module instantiations in the design.
Refer to the API Reference section to see the entire list of APIs that are used in the DM
Refer to the Object Diagrams section to learn how to traverse DM models.

Handles in NPI DM Model
The DM handle is an opaque reference to an object in the DM model. The DM model
provides functions that operate on objects referred to by handles. The particular
operations that are legal for an object referred to by a handle depend on the type of the
The NPI DM model contains two types of handles. Data type npiDmHandle represents a
handle referring to a DM object. Data type npiDmIter represents a handle referring to an
iterator object.
All of the possible relationships and properties that an object might have are documented
in the form of object diagrams.

Object Type Property
All objects have a npiDmType property, which is not shown in the data model diagrams.
npiDmObjType_e lists all object types.

Use npi_dm_property( npiDmType, <object_handle> ) to get an integer enum value that
represents the type of the object.
Use npi_dm_property_str( npiDmType, <object_handle> ) to get a pointer to a string
containing the enum name.
Other enum properties can be also obtained by both npi_dm_property and
npi_dm_property_str.

Keys to Object Model Diagrams
The keys to the symbols used in the data model diagrams are listed below.

3. Class definition: Bold letters in a dotted enclosure indicate a class definition, where
the class groups other objects and classes. Properties of the class are defined in this
location. The class definition can contain an object definition.

4. Class reference: Normal letters in a dotted enclosure indicate a class reference.

5. Unnamed class: A dotted enclosure with no name is an unnamed class. It is sometimes
convenient to group objects although they are not referenced as a group elsewhere;
therefore, a name is not indicated.

6. A single arrow indicates a one-to-one relationship accessed with the routine
npi_dm_handle().
For example: Given npiDmHandle variable ref_h of type ref, access obj_h of type Obj:
obj_h = npi_dm_handle(Obj, ref_h);

7. A tagged one-to-one relationship is traversed similarly, using Tag instead of Obj.
obj_h = npi_dm_handle(Tag, ref_h);

8. A double arrow indicates a one-to-many relationship accessed with the routine
npi_dm_iter_next().
For example: Given npiDmHandle variable ref_h of type ref, iterate objects of type Obj:
itr = npi_dm_iter_start(Obj, ref_h);

while (obj_h = npi_dm_iter_next(itr) )

9. A tagged one-to-many relationship is traversed similarly, using Tag instead of Obj.
itr = npi_dm_iter_start(Tag, ref_h);
while (obj_h = npi_dm_iter_next(itr) )

10. A one-to-many relationship that originates from a circle is traversed using NULL for the
itr = npi_dm_iter_start(Obj, NULL);
while (obj_h = npi_dm_iter_next(itr) )
/* process 'obj_h' *//

For object relationships (unless a special tag is shown in the diagram), the type used
for access is determined by the following steps:
a. Turn each word's first letter into an uppercase letter.
b. Add "npiDm" to the beginning of the word.
For example, if an application has a handle to a net and wants to go to the module
where the net is defined, the call would be as follows:
modH = npi_dm_handle( npiDmModule, netH );

Mix Language Support
* SystemVerilog on Top Example
* VHDL on Top Example

NPI DM Model supports mix language designs (SystemVerilog and VHDL). "SystemVerilog
on Top" means the instance in SystemVerilog is instantiated from the entity in VHDL.
"VHDL on Top" means the instance in VHDL is instantiated from the module in
SystemVerilog.

Refer to the object diagram of Instance, Port Instance, Parameter Instance and Vh
Instance.

SystemVerilog on Top Example
// top.v
logic [15:0] a;
logic [15:0] b;
logic [15:0] c;
add16 (.width(cv/2)) a1(a, b, c); -- npiDmInstance
-- add.vhd

entity add16 is -- npiDmVhEntity
generic(width: integer := 0); -- npiDmVhGeneric
port(ea : in std_logic_vector(15 downto 0); -- npiDmVhPort
eb : in std_logic_vector(15 downto 0); -- npiDmVhPort
esum : out std_logic_vector(15 downto 0)); -- npiDmVhPort
end entity add16;
architecture circuits of add16 is -- npiDmVhArchitecture
begin -- circuits of add16
end architecture circuits; -- of add16

On applying the "npiDmDefine" method to the npiDmInstance handle "a1", the
npiDmVhArchitecture handle "circuits" is returned.
* On applying the "npiDmVhEntity" method to the npiDmVhArchitecture handle "circuits",
the npiDmVhEntity handle "add16" is returned.
On applying the "npiDmParamInst" method to the npiDmInstance handle "a1", the
npiDmParamInst handle "width" is returned.
* On applying the "npiDmParameter" method to the npiDmParamInst handle "width", the
npiDmVhGeneric handle "width" is returned.
On applying the "npiDmPortInst" method to the npiDmInstance handle "a1", the
npiDmPortInst handles "ea", "eb" and "esum" are returned.
* On applying the "npiDmPort" method to the npiDmPortInst handle "ea", the
npiDmVhPort handle "ea" is returned.
* On applying the "npiDmPort" method to the npiDmPortInst handle "eb", the
npiDmVhPort handle "eb" is returned.
* On applying the "npiDmPort" method to the npiDmPortInst handle "esum", the
npiDmVhPort handle "esum" is returned.

VHDL on Top Example
// top.vhd

generic(width : integer :=0); -- npiDmVhGeneric
port(ea : in std_logic_vector(31 downto 0); -- npiDmVhPort
eb : in std_logic_vector(31 downto 0); -- npiDmVhPort
esum : out std_logic_vector(31 downto 0)); -- npiDmVhPort
end component add32;
-- component (instance/scope)
a0: add32 generic map(width => cv)
port map(ea => a, eb => b, esum => sum);
-- add.v
module add32(input [31:0] ea, input [31:0] eb, output [31:0] esum); -npiDmModule
parameter integer width = 0; -- npiDmParameter

On applying the "npiDmVhArchitecture" method to the npiDmVhInstance handle "a0", the
npiDmModule handle(modHdl) "add32" is returned.
On applying the "npiDmVhGenericMap" method to the npiDmVhInstance handle "a0",
one npiDmVhMapElem handle is returned.
* On applying the "npiDmVhFormal" method to the npiDmVhMapElem handle, the
npiDmVhGeneric handle(genericHdl) "width" is returned.
Use "npi_dm_handle_by_name(npi_dm_property_str(npiDmName, genericHdl), modHdl)"
to get the npiDmParameter handle "width".
On applying the "npiDmVhPortMap" method to the npiDmVhInstance handle "a0", three
npiDmVhMapElem handles are returned.
* On applying the "npiDmVhFormal" method to the first npiDmVhMapElem handle, the
npiDmVhPort handle(portHdl_1) "ea" is returned.
Use "npi_dm_handle_by_name(npi_dm_property_str(npiDmName, portHdl_1), modHdl)"
to get the npiDmPort handle "ea".
* On applying the "npiDmVhFormal" method to the second npiDmVhMapElem handle,
the npiDmVhPort handle(portHdl_2) "eb" is returned.
Use "npi_dm_handle_by_name(npi_dm_property_str(npiDmName, portHdl_2), modHdl)"
to get the npiDmPort handle "eb".
* On applying the "npiDmVhFormal" method to the second npiDmVhMapElem handle,
the npiDmVhPort handle(portHdl_3) "esum" is returned.
Use "npi_dm_handle_by_name(npi_dm_property_str(npiDmName, portHdl_3), modHdl)"
to get the npiDmPort handle "esum".

The NPI FSDB Model allows you to read the FSDB file with a set of convenient Tcl
commands or C APIs. You can get signal values in the FSDB with this model. Database
accessing performance and the programming usability are both considered in this model.
Refer to the API Reference section to see all the APIs that are used in the FSDB Model.

Handles in NPI FSDB Model
A handle is an opaque reference to an object in the FSDB model. The FSDB model
provides functions that operate on objects referred to by handles. The particular
operations that are legal for an object referred to by a handle depend on the object types.
The NPI FSDB model contains 6 types of handles:
1. npiFsdbFileHandle: a handle referring to a file object.
2. npiFsdbScopeHandle: a handle referring to a scope object.
3. npiFsdbSigHandle: a handle referring to a signal object.
4. npiFsdbSigdbHandle: a handle referring to a signal database object.
5. npiFsdbVctHandle: a handle referring to a value change traverse object.
6. npiFsdbScopeIter: a handle referring to a scope iterator object.
7. npiFsdbSigIter: a handle referring to a signal iterator object.
