Integration Process Overview
VC Apps Protocol Analyzer provides an open interface that enables integration of nonSynopsys VIPs (in-house or custom VIPs or other protocol-like components) into the Verdi
environment so as to facilitate access to the comprehensive protocol-specific debugging
capabilities provided by the Verdi platform.
In this flow, protocol-related data from these VIPs can be recorded into a common
FSDB file. This data is then processed in conjunction with a protocol extension definition
to enable the protocol-oriented debug and analysis capabilities of the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer.

Integration Process Overview

The VC Apps Protocol Analyzer integration process involves the following two steps:
1. In the first step, existing custom or in-house SystemVerilog VIP code is annotated
with calls to the VC Apps Protocol Analyzer SystemVerilog API. This is defined in the
verdi_pa_writer class that is delivered as part of the Verdi installation. This API
enables the recording of protocol-related activity to an FSDB file during simulation.
2. In the second step, you can create a protocol extension definition, which describes the
specific characteristics of the protocol information that was captured during simulation.

Protocol Objects and Object Types
Verdi Protocol Analyzer is a protocol-oriented debug and analysis environment. The goal
of the tool is to provide visualization and analysis of protocol objects. The term protocol
object refers to any description of data that is found in a protocol specification.
For example, consider a protocol specification that defines a packet object as a particular
sequence of bytes.
It defines a transfer object as a particular collection of packets.
In the Verdi Protocol Analyzer environment, packet and transfer are referred to as object
types.
The packets and transfers that are generated as a result of a particular simulation are
referred to as objects.
In other words, a protocol object definition is simply a way to associate a name with a
collection of data that is related in some way.
The motivation for defining object types in a protocol specification is to facilitate discussion
of the protocol features at various levels of abstraction.

Stacked Protocols or Abstraction Layers

The behavior of a protocol is expressed in terms of its own specific object types. Thus, the
first step to learn a new protocol is to become familiar with the structure and the behavior
of those protocol-specific object types and their relationships to one another.
Once an engineer becomes well-versed in the operation of a protocol, analysis or
debugging of protocol-specific behavior becomes most productive.
That productivity is highest when behavior is represented in terms of these protocolspecific objects.
In order to capitalize on such productivity, the Verdi Protocol Analyzer enables protocol
behavior to be explored in terms of protocol-specific objects and the relationships between
those objects.

Stacked Protocols or Abstraction Layers
The complexity of protocols varies greatly; for example, consider the vast difference in
complexity between a basic UART and a USB 3.0 host (or device). To fully explore the
capabilities of the Verdi Protocol Analyzer, this section examines a complex protocol.
Specifically, the SuperSpeed aspects of the USB 3.0 protocol.
The USB 3.0 protocol is a stacked protocol. This means that the behavior of the protocol
is defined across multiple layers. These layers are, from less abstract to more abstract the
physical layer, the link layer, and the protocol layer. Complex protocols are almost always
stacked. In contrast, a simple protocol is likely to be defined by only a single layer.
A protocol specification defines the activity that occurs in each layer. It also defines the
data that are associated with the activity of that layer. Additionally, the manner in which the
data is communicated between the layers.

Stacked Protocols or Abstraction Layers

For protocols with multiple layers, perhaps the most fundamental relationship between
protocol objects is the parent or child relationship. The relationship between the parent
object and the child objects is one of composition. The data model of the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer supports the specification of composite relationships. Thus, it understands the
complete relationship tree for any particular protocol object.
A protocol specification defines the object types associated with each level of abstraction.
The least abstract object types, that is, the objects types associated with the lowest level
of abstraction are likely to correspond closely to the signal patterns observed directly
on the protocol bus interface. Conversely, the most abstract object types are likely to
represent complex, high-level data objects that are far removed from the detailed bus
activity.
The following figure shows the fundamental object types defined by the USB 3.0 protocol.
It also shows the relationships between those object types in terms of their level of
abstraction. This type of figure is extremely useful for any protocol. It not only highlights
the protocol object types that are likely to be most useful when debugging protocol-related
issues, but it also suggests how the protocol data can be organized and presented.
Figure 6

USB 3.0 (SuperSpeed) Objects Organized by Level of Abstraction

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
For example, USB 3.0 (SuperSpeed) Objects Organized by Level of Abstraction shows
USB 3.0 objects that are captured by the Synopsys USB 3.0 VIP. The objects are
organized into three columns: labeled Transfers, Transactions, and Packets. These are
ordered from left to right by decreasing level of abstraction.
This approach of organizing protocol activity according to the level of abstraction makes
it easy to analyze protocol-related issues in the most efficient manner. Some issues can
be most easily observed and understood at a very high level of abstraction. Other issues
might require analysis at lower levels of abstraction.
For most protocols, the data objects that are manipulated in each layer can be considered
as (and thus represented by) transactions. Ideally, a VIP captures the activity related to
any of these objects. As previously discussed, the data should be organized according to
the abstraction layer with which the data is associated.
There might be additional activity of interest that aids the protocol debug process. For
example, the USB 3.0 protocol defines a state machine (called the LTSSM) that resides
in the link layer. The ability to capture and display the LTSSM state can greatly accelerate

the debug process. For example, to identify a scenario where the LTSSM is stuck in a
particular state.
Another example of additional activity of interest that aids the debug of USB 3.0 scenarios
is the behavior of the Low-Frequency Periodic Signaling (LFPS) transmitter and receiver.
These are primarily used to establish the initial communication between a host and a
device and for low-power activities.
Note that both of these items are shown in the previous figure, and are located in the
figure according to their relative level of abstraction. Ideally, a VIP captures this additional
protocol-related data.

Parent or Child Relationships
For any stacked protocol and even for many simple protocols, there is a hierarchical
relationship between objects. For example, for USB 3.0, a transfer is composed of one
or more transactions. A transaction is composed of multiple packets; and a packet is
represented by a specific sequence of symbols. As USB 3.0 supports multiple concurrent
transfers and transactions, it is extremely important to understand the relationship
between these objects when debugging.

Hierarchical Object Types
An additional complexity is that the object types (such as transfers, transactions, packets,
and symbols in the case of USB 3.0) are rarely monolithic. It is common for objects of a
particular type to have multiple possible representations. For example, there are different
kinds of USB 3.0 transfers, transactions, packets, and so on. When debugging a protocol,
it is not only important to know the type of each object. It is also important to be able to
distinguish between the various sub-types of objects of a particular type.
USB 3.0 (SuperSpeed) Objects Organized by Level of Abstraction provided a comparative
view of the base object types (such as transfers, transactions, and packets). These base
object types are used to define the general behavior of the protocol.
Each object type is used to discuss a common set of functionality. For the majority of these
object types, the protocol also defines more strictly-defined variations of the object type
that are applicable to a specific task. In a protocol extension, each variation is referred to
as an object sub-type. This is equivalent to a specialization in the software realm.
Note that in Hierarchical Relationships Between Objects Shown in the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer, the four child objects are shown in the lower-right portion. Even though the child
objects are all USB 3.0 transactions, each is a different kind of transaction. Also note that
these transactions have different labels: SETUP, OUT, and STATUS. These three object
types are examples of USB 3.0 transaction object sub-types.
In the USB 3.0 protocol, there is not only an object type hierarchy for transactions, there
is also an object type hierarchy for packets. A packet is a base object type, with certain
characteristics. However, the protocol later describes four different packet sub-types: Link
Management Packet (LMP), Transaction Packet (TP), Data Packet (DP), and Isochronous
Timestamp Packet (ITP). Two of these packet sub-types (LMPs and TPs) also have a
number of sub-types.
The following figure shows all of the different USB 3.0 packet object types and how they
relate to one another:

Hierarchical Object Sub-Type Relationships for USB 3.0 (SuperSpeed) Packets

Object Fields or Attributes

For any particular protocol, the object type hierarchy can be multiple levels deep,
depending on the complexity of the protocol.

Object Fields or Attributes
Any data associated with the operation of the protocol defines the attributes that provide
detailed information about the specific protocol objects that are captured.
At the most basic level, each object that is captured by the VIP must have attributes to
specify the start time, the end time, and the type of object for use during debug.
In addition, protocol specifications typically define other attributes that are associated with
the different object types that are manipulated by the protocol.
For example, USB 3.0 transaction packets have a number of associated attributes, such
as an endpoint number and a sequence number.
Even though these attributes are ultimately represented by a number of bits in the
transaction object, it is much easier to debug transaction-related issues when the values of
these attributes are easily observable.
Figure 10

The ability to view the values of object attributes is an essential aid to debug protocolrelated issues.
Not only are these attributes made available for analysis, each attribute is typed to provide
robust search and filtering capabilities within the Verdi Protocol Analyzer debugging
environment.
That is, by typing an attribute as an integer, a [simulation] time, a floating-point number, or
a string (for example), sophisticated searching and filtering capabilities can be provided.
For example, applying comparison operators (such as '<' and '>') to an attribute whose
values are represented as strings can produce completely different results.
The same operators applied to an attribute (with the same values) whose values are
represented as integers can produce different results.

Predecessor or Successor Relationships

Predecessor or Successor Relationships
Hierarchical relationships are previously discussed. These are composite relationships,
as they describe how one object is composed of other objects. This document uses the
familiar term for a composite relationship: a parent/child relationship.
But some protocols can have a different kind of relationship between objects that is causal
in nature. In other words, one object is the reason for (or cause of) the creation of one or
more other objects. The more familiar term for a composite relationship is a predecessor/
successor relationship.
To explain the value of being able to visualize such relationships, a different protocol
is considered. Namely ACE (AXI Coherence Extensions) of the AMBA 4 protocol from
ARM. This protocol enables system-level cache coherency across clusters of multicore processors. That is, the system can use multiple components that each has a local
memory cache. The use of a local cache can greatly increase the performance of an
individual component.
However, to maintain high performance of the overall system, it is necessary to ensure the
caches of the various local components are synchronized. It is also necessary to maximize
the use of cached data across the system, so as to minimize access to the main memory,
which is comparatively expensive in terms of performance.
In the AMBA 4 protocol, these coherency checks and optimizations are performed
by a system interconnect. The various components are connected along with special
transactions called snoop transactions. These snoop transactions enables the system
interconnect to query other components about their local cached data.
For example, a simple AMBA 4 might contain two components, each of which has a
cache. These two components are connected to the system interconnect, along with the
main memory. If the first component needs to read the value of a particular variable, it
issues a read transaction and transmits that transaction to the system interconnect.
The system interconnect, in turn, generates a snoop transaction and transmits that
transaction to the second component. This is essentially to "ask" that component if it
already has a valid value for the variable of interest. The second component generates a
snoop response transaction. This response either includes the requested data or indicates
that it does not have that data in its cache. In the latter scenario, the system interconnect
reads the requested data from the main memory and sends that data back to the first
component.
While many details of the ACE protocol are omitted from the explanation above,
the purpose of the example is to highlight the relationship between the two types of
transactions that were introducedin that explanation: read transactions and snoop
transactions.

Channels

In the scenario described, the snoop transaction is generated as a result of the read
transaction. That is, the read transaction caused the creation of the snoop transaction. The
AMBA 4 protocol supports multiple, concurrent read transactions, and write transactions.
Due to this complexity, it is useful to understand the relationship between coherent nonsnoop transactions and the corresponding snoop transactions that are generated by the
system interconnect.

Channels
Verdi Protocol Analyzer must be aware of the object type hierarchy to be able to display
the protocol objects in the most meaningful manner for the debugging process. For
example, all packets should be grouped together, independent of their sub-type.
However, in the following figure, note that not all packet objects are displayed in a single
row; there are two rows, labeled Rx and Tx. In Verdi Protocol Analyzer, these sub-rows are
referred to as channels, and provide a mechanism for separating objects of the same base
object type into separate groups (which are then displayed in separate rows). In this case,
the Rx channel displays packets that are received by the USB VIP and the Tx channel
displays packets that the USB VIP has transmitted.

Low-Level Memory Data
There are two types of low-level memory activity that can be written to the FSDB and
visualized in the Memory Protocol Analyzer:
* Front door memory actions that refer to memory activity initiated by changes to the bus
(that is, as a result of pin wiggles)
* Back door memory actions that refer to memory activity initiated by the test
environment.
The difference between front door and back door memory access is illustrated in the
following figure:
Figure 12

Front Door and Back Door Memory Access

Memories are passive components. In other words, memories do not generate activity on
their own. Memories respond to requests that are made using the memory bus.
There are two kinds of front door memory operations: memory read operations and
memory write operations.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
sive components. In other words, memories do not generate activity on
their own. Memories respond to requests that are made using the memory bus.
There are two kinds of front door memory operations: memory read operations and
memory write operations. Memory write operations can be further sub-divided into
normal writes and masked writes. A masked write is the equivalent of a read-modify-write
operation.
Since this is now a relatively common feature of contemporary memories, the VC Apps
Protocol Analyzer APIs support these two types of write operations and can distinguish
between them. Thus, there are different memory actions for these two types of write
operations. There are three front door memory actions: read, write, and write_masked.
However, a robust memory VIP should provide a verification engineer with other ways
to access the memory without having to access the memory bus. For example, a
memory VIP should provide a mechanism for retrieving a value from memory for use in a
scoreboard. It should also allow injecting an incorrect data value into a specific memory
location. It should also be possible for the test environment to quickly initialize a memory
with a pattern or with data from a file.

Initializing a Memory Using a Pattern
A memory (or a portion of a memory) can be initialized from the test environment (that is,
with a back door memory action) using a pattern.
The following table describes the types of initialization patterns that are supported by the
VC Apps Protocol Analyzer APIs:
Pattern Type

CONST

Initialize the memory (or address range) with the
specified constant value.

INCR

Initialize the memory (or address range) starting with
the specified value and increment the value for each
subsequent address.

DECR

Initialize the memory (or address range) starting with
the specified value and decrement the value for each
subsequent address.

WALK_LEFT

Initialize the memory (or address range) starting with
the specified value and rotate the value left by one for
each subsequent address.

WALK_RIGHT

Initialize the memory (or address range) starting with
the specified value. Rotate the value right by one for
each subsequent address.

Pattern Type

RAND

Initialize the memory (or address range) to random
values. Because patterns are virtual, the actual random
value is not assigned unless a read or peek memory
action is performed on an address in the specified
range.

Loading Memory Data From a File
There are two memory actions associated with loading memory data from a file. The
load_file memory action records the name of the file from which the data is being read.
This memory action must be created before recording memory actions for individual data
values.

Correlating Memory Transactions With Memory Actions
For Synopsys Memory VIPs, it is possible to synchronize high-level memory protocol
transactions with the subsequent front door memory actions. When selection
synchronization is enabled in both Protocol Analyzer and Memory Protocol Analyzer, the
selection of a protocol transaction causes a memory action to be selected, and vice-versa.

This selection synchronization is shown in the following figure:
Figure 16
Selection Synchronization Between High-Level Memory Transactions and
Low-Level Memory Actions

This selection synchronization is also available for custom memory VIPs, but it requires
that certain conventions be followed. As illustrated in the previous figure, the following two
rules must be followed:
* For read memory protocol transactions, the corresponding read memory action must
be recorded at the time the protocol transaction is started.
* For write memory protocol transactions, the corresponding write (or write_masked)
memory action must be recorded at the time the protocol transaction is ended.
These two rules ensure that time is synchronized correctly between the two windows. In
order to synchronize the memory address between the two windows, the memory protocol
transaction must have an attribute called logical_address. The value of logical_address
should be the address of the memory location with which the high-level transaction is
associated.
Selection synchronization only works if all of these rules are followed.

Integration Process
VC Apps Protocol Analyzer provides an open interface that enables integration of nonSynopsys VIPs (in-house or custom VIPs or other protocol-like components) into the Verdi
environment so as to facilitate access to the comprehensive protocol-specific debugging
capabilities provided by the Verdi platform.
In this flow, protocol-related data from these VIPs can be recorded into a common
FSDB file. This data is then processed in conjunction with a protocol extension definition
to enable the protocol-oriented debug and analysis capabilities of the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer.
The VC Apps Protocol Analyzer integration process involves the following two steps:
1. In the first step, existing custom or in-house SystemVerilog VIP code is annotated
with calls to the VC Apps Protocol Analyzer SystemVerilog API, which is defined in
the verdi_pa_writer class that is delivered as part of the Verdi installation. This API
enables the recording of protocol-related activity to an FSDB file during simulation.
2. In the second step, you can create a protocol extension definition, which describes the
specific characteristics of the protocol information that was captured during simulation.
This section describes about the following topics:
* Data Recorded During Simulation
* Protocol Characteristics
* Protocol Analysis and Object Type Identification

Data Recorded During Simulation
The following protocol-related information is recorded during simulation for the instances
of the VIPs that are configured to capture such data:
* General VIP information
The location of the VIP in the design hierarchy (that is, the instance path of the
VIP).
The name of the protocol with which the VIP is associated.

Protocol Characteristics

The version of the protocol with which the VIP is associated.
For memory instances, address, data width, and the memory access type.
* Protocol transactions or objects
The common attributes of the transaction or object (start time, end time, object type,
and channel name).
Multiple, typed object attributes (with optional expected values).
Optional composite (that is, parent or child) relationships with other objects.
Optional causal (that is, predecessor or successor) relationships with other objects.
* Memory data
Front door and back door memory actions.

Protocol Characteristics
The following general protocol information is captured as part of the protocol extension
definition. Note that this information is captured once for a particular protocol as part of
the integration process and is used by the Verdi Protocol Analyzer when processing data
from any instance of that protocol.
* General protocol information
The name and the version of the protocol.
The visual attributes of the protocol, such as, display text, a brief description, and
an icon.
* Optional information about methodologies supported by the VIP
The name of the methodology (UVM, OVM, UVM, HDL).
The visual attributes of the methodology, such as, display text and a brief
description.
An optional base path or URL that indicates the location of methodology-specific
help.
* Optional general protocol and VIP help resources
2. More specifically, this information described in a protocol extension definition is captured for a particular version
of a protocol. Protocol definitions can change over time. Also, the information that is captured by a VIP can
change over time. These possibilities are supported by the Verdi Protocol Analyzer through versioning of the
protocol extension definitions.

Protocol Characteristics

The name of the help resource.
The visual attributes of the help resource, such as, display text and a brief
description.
The path or URL that indicates the location of the help resource.
The methodology name with which the help resource is associated, if appropriate.
* Protocol object type definitions
The name of the object type.
The visual attributes of the object type, such as, display text, a brief description, an
icon, and drawing attributes (background color, border color, font color).
The relative display order of the object type.
An optional SystemVerilog class name used by the VIP to represent the object type.
Optional object type help resources (object type help resources have the same
characteristics as previously listed protocol or VIP help resources).
Optional protocol object type attribute definitions (see next item).
An optional list of protocol object sub-types (that is, names of other object types).
* Protocol object type attribute definitions
The name of the object type attribute (also used as the display text).
The data type of the object type attribute (in SystemVerilog format).
A brief description of the object type attribute.
Optional object type attribute help resources (object type attribute help resources
have the same characteristics as previously listed protocol or VIP help resources).
* Signal interface groups
The name of the signal group.
The name of the signal interface with which the signal group is associated.
The visual attributes of the signal group, such as, the display text and a brief
description.
The list of signals in the signal group and option radix information for each signal.

Protocol Analyzer technology can be viewed as being essentially protocol-agnostic. This
idea can be most easily understood by considering the basic characteristics of the object

The display and the analysis capabilities of the Verdi Protocol Analyzer can be applied

In other words, any activity of interest with respect to the operation of the VIP should be

Some examples of such activity are as follows:
* Transitions of internal state machines.
* State changes for other internal structures (such as, reaching the high/low watermarks
of a FIFO).
* Reconfigurations that modify the behavior of the VIP.

be viewed as having a start and end time, even if that activity is not represented by the

Thus, the first step of the integration process is to evaluate the protocol and the VIP to
identify the types of objects associated with the protocol and the VIP. The goal of this step
is to identify the protocol-related data that most enhances protocol-oriented debug and
analysis productivity.
During this process, note the following points:
* Consider both big picture protocol-centric debugging and the detailed protocol analysis.
* List any activity of interest that aids protocol debug.
* Start by listing transactions (on the VIP or layer boundaries).
* Consider other internal activity and processing performed by the VIP.
* Consider the relationships between objects (both parent/child and predecessor/
successor).
Once the top-level object types are identified, the next step in the process is to sub-divide
each of the top-level object types into object type hierarchies.

The following figure shows the complete object type hierarchy for the packet object type
(that is, for both SuperSpeed and USB 2.0), as defined in the protocol extension definition
of the Synopsys USB 3.0 VIP:
Figure 19

Complete packet Object Type Hierarchy for Synopsys USB 3.0 VIP

An object type hierarchy is analogous to a class hierarchy. Child object types (or subtypes) are variants of their parent type. For example, a Port Cfg Resp packet is also an
LMP packet, an SS Packet, and a Packet.
An object type hierarchy can greatly simplify protocol debug. Different packet sub-types
have different display text. This text is drawn within the rectangle that represents each
packet in the timeline display within the Protocol Analyzer. Different object types can
also have different colors. Different colors can be used to indicate different behavior. For
example, for both SuperSpeed and USB 2.0 packets, bad responses (NRDY and NAK,
respectively) are drawn in a light red color, whereas good responses (ACK and ERDY)
are drawn in a light green color. Using this differentiation, the general flow of traffic can be
quickly ascertained with a quick look at the timeline display.
A robust object type hierarchy also enhances searching, filtering, and general analysis
capabilities that are available in the Protocol Analyzer. For example, the timeline display
can be easily configured to only display certain types of packets. The object type hierarchy
and the number of objects of each type are also shown in the Summary tab.

Figure 20

Summary Tab Showing Object Type Hierarchy and Number of Each Object Type

Even if all of the different kinds of packets are represented in the VIP by a single
SystemVerilog class, the different kinds of packets can still be recorded as different object
types when they are written to the FSDB.
For example, if a single class is used to represent every kind of packet, but that class
includes a field to distinguish the various kinds of packets (perhaps defined using an
enumerated type) The code that is added to the VIP to record packets can check the
value of that field and assign the appropriate corresponding object type when creating the
packet object.

Directory Structure and Files
For each protocol that is integrated with the Verdi Protocol Analyzer, there is information
about the protocol that only needs to be captured once. This information is stored in a
collection of files, referred to as the protocol extension definition. The overall directory
structure and files that comprise a protocol extension definition are described this chapter.
The purpose of a protocol extension definition is to provide the Verdi Protocol Analyzer
with protocol-specific information . This enables the tool to organize and display the
protocol-related data that was generated during a simulation. The organization and display
are tailored to support protocol-oriented debugging.
The extension definition for each protocol is contained in a directory structure. The name
of the top-most directory is the internal name of the protocol. This name cannot contain
any spaces or non-alphanumeric characters, with the exception of underscore (`_')
characters. For simplicity, it is recommended to use all lower-case letters. To avoid naming
collisions, consider adding a prefix or suffix that clearly differentiates the protocol name
(such as, snps_xyzbus or xyzbus_snps).
When a VIP (or other SystemVerilog code) is annotated using the verdi_pa_writer
class, the protocol name that is specified in the class constructor must match the name
that is specified for the top-level of the protocol extension definition directory.
Figure 23

Directory Structure for a Protocol Extension Definition

The next level in the directory structure of the protocol extension definition is a subdirectory that represents the version of the protocol extension definition.

Chapter 4: Directory Structure and Files

Every protocol extension definition is versioned. This enables changes or enhancements
to be made to a protocol extension definition without the risk of breaking the existing
flows of current users. For example, a VIP might be enhanced to capture additional
protocol-related data during simulation. This new data might come from new features that
are added to the protocol over time. Alternatively, the new data might come from enduser requests that additional information be captured during simulation. Either of these
scenarios would certainly require modifications to the protocol extension definition.
The version string cannot contain any spaces or non-alphanumeric characters, with the
exception of underscore (`_') and dot (`.') characters. For simplicity, it is recommended
to use all lower-case letters. While any version string is permitted, a simple versioning
scheme is recommended (such as, 1.0, 1.1, 2.0_beta, 2.0, and so on).
For each version of the VIP that has been annotated using the verdi_pa_writer class,
there should be a corresponding version of a protocol extension definition for that VIP. This
means that there should be a sub-directory whose name is the same as the version string
passed to the verdi_pa_writer constructor in the VIP SystemVerilog code.
Note that when a VIP (or other SystemVerilog code) is annotated using the
verdi_pa_writer class, both the protocol name and the protocol version are specified in
the class constructor.

As shown in Directory Structure for a Protocol Extension Definition, there is a symbolic
link called "latest" at the same level in the directory structure as the extension definition
versions. The version of the protocol extension definition that this link points to indicates
the default version of the extension definition.
This link is only used if there is no directory that corresponds to the information captured
during simulation. There is no directory that corresponds the version reported by the
VIP. If the versions of both the annotated VIPs and the protocol extension definitions
are managed appropriately, this situation should not occur. Also, note that under these
conditions, errors or warnings might be generated when the data is read into the Verdi
Protocol Analyzer.
Within the version sub-directory is another sub-directory that must be called pa. This
additional layer is included in the directory hierarchy to separate information related to

Chapter 4: Directory Structure and Files

the Verdi Protocol Analyzer from any other protocol-related data. While this is completely
optional, this allows the protocol extension definition directory structure to be used as a
common location to store other protocol-related files, such as, documentation, code, or
any other data, if needed.
The pa directory contains the following two items:
* A file - extension.xml. The extension.xml file is an XML file (as implied by its extension)
and defines all of the protocol-related information required by the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer.
* A subdirectory - icons. The icons directory contains icons that provide visual
representations for protocol-specific object types that are defined for the protocol.
These icons are used by the Verdi Protocol Analyzer throughout the GUI to provide
visual cues to aid protocol debug.

Location of Protocol Extension Definitions
Protocol extension definitions can reside in one or more directories. These directories are
specified by setting the value of the PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH environment variable. Multiple
directory paths can be specified using the colon character (:) as a delimiter.

Location of Protocol Extension Definitions

Figure 26

Multiple Protocol Extension Definitions in Multiple Locations

Multiple Protocol Extension Definitions in Multiple Locations shows four protocol extension
definitions, represented as <protocol_1>, <protocol_2>, <protocol_3>, and <protocol_4>.
The protocol extension definitions for <protocol_1> and <protocol_2> are located in a
directory represented by <directory_a>.
The protocol extension definitions for <protocol_3> and <protocol_4> are located in a
directory represented by <directory_b>.
For this scenario, the PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH environment variable must be set as follows:
%setenv PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH <directory_a>:<directory_b>

The value of the PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH environment variable must be set before invoking
the Verdi Protocol Analyzer.

Protocol Extension XML File
The protocol extension file (extension.xml), which resides in the pa sub-directory of a
protocol extension definition is an XML file (as implied by its extension) and defines all of
the protocol-related information required by the Verdi Protocol Analyzer.
Since this file resides in the pa sub-directory, which itself resides in the version subdirectory of a protocol directory, the extension file defines the characteristics of a specific
version of a protocol.
The extension file uses a standard XML (eXtensible Markup Language) format. XML is a
"human-readable" (that is, ACSII) format that appears very similar to HTML.
This chapter does not explain all the details of what can be specified using XML, as the
extension file only uses the simplest XML constructs. However, this chapter attempts to
explain enough of the "basics" of XML, so that an extension file can be constructed without
the need for external research.
This chapter contains the following sections:
* XML Basics
* General Protocol Information
* Supported Methodologies
* Protocol or Methodology Help Resources
* Object Types or Object Type Hierarchies
* Object Type Fields or Attributes
* Signal Interface Groups

XML Basics
As previously mentioned, the extension.xml file uses the XML format. XML is ASCIIbased, and thus can be created and modified with any text editor. The extension file
can be created "brute force", by just typing in the constructs described in this document.
However, this document has an appendix that describes tools and methods that can be

XML Basics

used to simplify the construction and validation of protocol extension files. The review of
this appendix is highly encouraged.
Many of the details that are described in this section are managed by tools that are freely
available on the Internet. nonetheless, the basics of the XML format are described in this
document : for completeness, for help with understanding issues or problems that are
encountered, and for those who might simply choose to use their favorite text editor (that
might not provide specific support for XML).
Every XML document should begin with an XML declaration, which describes the XML
format:

The data described by the XML file is specified using tags, elements, and attributes.
A tag is a string that begins with the less than (<) character and ends with the greater than
(>) character. There are three kinds of tags: start tags, end tags, and empty element tags.
Start tags contain strings that can contain only alphanumeric characters and underscores,
such as <protocol> (the exact restrictions are more complex than this, but all of the tags
that appear in an extension file follow this rule). End tags are similar, but also include

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
ings that can contain only alphanumeric characters and underscores,
such as <protocol> (the exact restrictions are more complex than this, but all of the tags
that appear in an extension file follow this rule). End tags are similar, but also include
a forward slash (/) character after the starting < character, such as </protocol>. Empty
element tags are also similar to start tags, but include a space and a forward slash before
the ending > character, such as <help_resource />.
An element is an XML construct that either has matching start and end tags or is an empty
element tag (such as <protocol> </protocol> and <help_resource />). Elements that are
defined with matching start and end tags can include content between those tags. This
enables XML to describe hierarchical data relationships. Elements that are included within
other elements are referred to as child elements.
An attribute is a name-value pair that can be defined within a start tag or an empty
element tag. Attribute names can only contain alphanumeric characters and underscores.
The attribute value is specified after the attribute name using an equals (=) character,
followed by a string that must be enclosed within double-quotes (`"').

While this section provides a very simplified introduction to XML, it provides the basic
information that is needed to construct a protocol extension file.

General Protocol Information
The protocol element is the outermost element of the protocol extension XML structure.
The values of the attributes associated with this element are used to specify general
information about the protocol.

Supported Methodologies

The attributes associated with the protocol element are shown in the following table (all
three of these attributes are required ):

name

The "internal" name of the protocol, which should be
the same as the name of the top-most directory of the
protocol extension definition

display_text

The text to display when information pertaining to the
protocol is shown in the UI

description

A brief (that is, usually one-line) description of the
protocol

The following XML code shows the outer-most structure of a protocol extension XML file:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plugin>
<extension point="com.synopsys.sg.vip.pa.protocol">
<!-Verdi Protocol Analyzer Extension Definition
for Synopsys SuperFast Protocol (version 1.1)
-->
<protocol name="snps_sfp"
display_text="Synopsys SFP"
description="Synopsys SuperFast Protocol VIP">
</protocol>
</extension>
</plugin>

All other information about the protocol is represented as child elements of the protocol
element. Each of these elements is described in the sections that follow.

Supported Methodologies
The methodology element describes the attributes of each methodology that is supported
by the VIP.
For example, most Synopsys VIPs support multiple methodologies, such as, UVM, OVM,
VMM, and HDL.
The latter enables the VIP to be inserted into a "pure Verilog" verification environment.
3. The names of optional attributes are drawn in the attribute tables in italics. The section that contains the table
also discusses whether an attribute is required or optional (and, if optional, the condition under which it should be
defined). The italic text simply provides a simple visual queue when referencing this document at a later time.

Supported Methodologies

The attributes associated with the methodology element are shown in the following table:

name

The "logical" name of the methodology that the VIP
supports. Currently, the value of this attribute is
restricted to "uvm", "ovm", "vmm", or "hdl".

display_text

The text to display when information pertaining to the
methodology is shown within the UI.

description

A brief (that is, usually one-line) description of the
methodology (this can provide clarity to the user within
the UI, if needed)

base_help_url

The location of the base folder (or URL) for class
reference documentation. (The use of this attribute is
described in detail later in this document)

The name, display_text, and description attributes must be specified for each
methodology.
The base_help_url attribute is optional (more on this topic later).
The following XML code shows methodology elements for a VIP that supports two
methodologies (UVM and OVM).
These two elements are located within the outer-most protocol element.
The protocol element has been truncated and drawn in gray to highlight the methodology
definitions.
<protocol >
<!-- Supported Methodologies -->
<methodology name="uvm"
display_text="UVM"
description="Universal Verification Methodology"
base_help_url="$VIP_HOME/sfp/1.1/doc/uvm/html/" />
<methodology name="ovm"
display_text="OVM"
description="Open Verification Methodology"
base_help_url="$VIP_HOME/sfp/1.1/doc/ovm/html/" />
</protocol>

Protocol or Methodology Help Resources

The base_help_url attribute is an optional attribute that can provide the following two
benefits:
* Firstly, it greatly simplifies the process of defining help resources for common protocol
items.
Examples include object types and the fields (that is, attributes) that are associated
with object types.
* Secondly, for VIPs that support multiple protocols, it also simplifies access to those
help resources from within the Verdi Protocol Analyzer.
The details of this mechanism are discussed in a later section of this document,
specifically in the sections that describe how to define object types and their associated
fields.
For each methodology that the VIP supports, there should be a corresponding
methodology element in the extension definition.
Even if the VIP that is being defined only supports one methodology (UVM, for example), a
corresponding methodology element should still be added to the extension definition.

Protocol or Methodology Help Resources
During the debug process, it is important to have easy access to help resources. Help
resources can be general or specific to a VIP. Further, VIP-specific help might only apply to
a particular methodology, such as, UVM or OVM.
The help resources that are defined in a protocol extension can reference any file that can
be viewed in a browser or PDF viewer. Further, the help resource can reference a "local"
file or an "external" URL. Some examples of help resources are VIP manuals, VIP class
reference material, Application notes, methodology guides, and user group sites.
The help_resource element defines a help resource using the attributes shown in the
following table:

methodology

The methodology with which the help resource is
associated. This attribute is optional and should not be
specified for general help resources. The value of this
attribute is restricted to "uvm", "ovm", "vmm" or "hdl".

name

The internal name to use when referring to the help
resource. This name cannot contain any spaces or
non-alphanumeric characters, with the exception of
underscore (`_') characters. For simplicity, the use of all
lower-case letters is recommended.

Protocol or Methodology Help Resources

display_text

The text to display when information pertaining to the
help resource is shown within the UI.

description

A brief (that is, usually one-line) description of the help

Protocol or Methodology Help Resources

display_text

The text to display when information pertaining to the
help resource is shown within the UI.

description

A brief (that is, usually one-line) description of the help
resource (this can provide clarity to the user within the
UI, if needed).

location

The location of the help resource. This can be a path to
a file or a URL and can include environment variables.

The name, display_text, description, and location attributes must be specified for each
help resource. As noted in the table, the methodology attribute is optional and should only
be specified for methodology-specific help resources.
The following XML code shows specifications for two general protocol help resources.
Note that these two elements are located within the outer-most protocol element. The
protocol element has been truncated and drawn in gray to highlight the methodology
definitions.
<protocol >
<!-- General Protocol Help Resources -->
<help_resource name="release_notes"
display_text="SFP VIP Release Notes"
description="Synopsys SuperFast Protocol VIP
Release Notes"
location
="$VIP_HOME/sfp/1.1/doc/spf_release_notes.pdf" />
<help_resource name="solvNetPlus"
display_text="Synopsys SolvNetPlus"
description="Access to Synopsys SolvNetPlus on-line
help resources"
location="https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com" />
</protocol>

Note that the location of the first help resource is a local file whose location is determined
by the value of an environment variable and the location of the second help resource is a
URL.
The following XML code shows specifications for two methodology-specific help
resources:
<protocol >
<!-- Methodology-Specific Help Resources -->

Protocol or Methodology Help Resources

<help_resource methodology="uvm"
name="uvm_user_manual"
display_text="SFP VIP UVM User Manual"
description="Synopsys SuperFast Protocol VIP UVM User
Manual"
location
="$VIP_HOME/sfp/1.1/doc/spf_uvm_user_manual.pdf" />
<help_resource methodology="ovm"
name="ovm_user_manual"
display_text="SFP VIP OVM User Manual"
description="Synopsys SuperFast Protocol VIP OVM User
Manual"
location
="$VIP_HOME/sfp/1.1/doc/spf_ovm_user_manual.pdf" />
</protocol>

Both general protocol and methodology-specific help resources can be accessed from the
Protocols tab in the Verdi Protocol Analyzer.
HTML help resources can be opened either in a tab which is internal to the Protocol
Analyzer or in an external browser, depending on the user's preference settings.

The object_type element defines an object type using the attributes shown in the following
table:

name

The internal name to use when referring to the object type. This
name cannot contain any spaces or non-alphanumeric characters,
with the exception of underscore (`_') characters. For simplicity, the
use of all lower-case letters is recommended.

display_text

The text to display when information pertaining to the object type is
shown within the UI.

description

A brief (usually one-line) description of the object type (this can
provide clarity to the user within the UI, if needed). The description
can also be defined using a sub-element. This approach is shown in
the example that follows.

background_color
border_color

font_color

The background color to use when drawing objects of this type in the
timeline and other displays (such as, search results).
The border color to use when drawing objects of this type.
The font color to use when drawing objects of this type.

icon

The location of the icon to use to represent this object type. The icon
should be a 16x16 PNG image located in the "icons" sub-directory.

relative_display_order

An integer that indicates the location of this object type relative to
other object types in the same hierarchy or sub-hierarchy when
drawn in the timeline display or lists.

show_field_in_timeline An optional list of comma-separated attributes, whose values are

drawn in the rectangles that represent objects of this type in the
timeline display. This attribute is inherited for object sub-types (so it is
not necessary to copy this attribute in all object sub-types).
class_name

header_text

An optional attribute, whose value is the name of the SystemVerilog
class with which this object type is associated.
The text to display in the column of the timeline display. The
header_text attribute is required for top-level object types, but has no
meaning for object sub-types.

Note:
Colors are represented as a six digit hexadecimal number in the form
RRGGBB. "RR" represents red, "GG" represents green and "BB" represents
blue. Red, green, and blue values can range from "00" (0) to "FF" (255). For
example, "000000" represents black and "FFFFFF" represents white. Colors
must be specified for top-level object types. If color attributes are not specified
for an object sub-type, its colors are inherited from its parent object type.

text: Sample Object Type Definition Showing Attributes and General Sub-Element

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Note that in the previous example, the description is not declared as an attribute. For
object types, the description can be defined using either an attribute, or alternately can be
defined using a sub-element. If the description sub-element is used, the text attribute is
used to define the description:
<description text="MIPI CSI2 Packet" />

In the previous example, other sub-elements are shown (however, with their attributes
omitted). These optional sub-elements define help resources, fields, and object sub-types.

Two example help resources for the svt_mipi_csi2_packet object type are shown below.
The other details of the object type definition have been removed or truncated for clarity.
The methodology definitions for the protocol VIP are also shown in the following figure:
Figure 30

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text: Example Object Type Help Resource that Utilizes Optional "methodology"

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
During the debug process, if a problem appears to be related to a packet object, having
easy access to the help resources associated with the packet object type would be very
useful. However, the location of the help resource might be methodology-dependent.
Further, the location of the help resources might include deep directory paths, whose
duplication is error-prone. The base_help_url attribute associated with the methodology
element can help address these issues.
The methodology that was used to generate simulation data can be set when the resulting
data is viewed in the Verdi Protocol Analyzer. If the methodology is set, only the "pertinent"
help resources are shown. The pertinent help resources includes the following:
* pertinent Help resources that do not specify the optional methodology attribute.
* pertinent Help resources that do specify the methodology attribute and match the
methodology specified for the design.
If the methodology element defines the option base_help_url attribute, that attribute is
prepended to the "location" specified in the help_resource element.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
For example, using the data in the previous figure, if the methodology for the design is
set to UVM and help is requested for an object whose type is svt_mipi_csi2_packet, the
following help page is displayed:
$DESIGNWARE_HOME/vip/svt/mipi_svt/J-2014.12/doc/mipi_csi2_svt_uvm/html/cl
ass_svt_mipi_csi2_packet.html

title: Verification ContinuumTM

If no methodology is set for the design, both UVM and VMM help resources are presented
for the user to select from.
In the previous example, there are separate help resource definitions for each
methodology. This is only necessary if there is a need to have a different value for
description, display_text, or location attributes for each help resource. For the previous
example, if the description attribute was changed to MIPI CSI2 Packet Class Reference,
only one help resource definition would be needed.
The ability to define object type hierarchies is a key feature of the Verdi Protocol Analyzer.
Object sub types are specified using the object_sub_type element. This element must be
contained within an object_type element. Forward referencing is permitted. An object type
can refer to the name of another object type that has not yet been defined in the extension
file.
The object_type element uses a single attribute called name, as shown in the following
example:
Figure 31

General Structure of Object Sub type Definitions

Note that the object in the first column is an object of type svt_mipi_csi2_hs_packet, as the
text HS is displayed on the object. This object is drawn in the Packets column because its
object type is a sub-type of svt_mipi_csi2_packet.This is a top-level object type and thus
results in the creation of a column.

Object Type Fields or Attributes

Note that all object_type elements are child elements of the protocol element. Deeper
object type hierarchies can be created by including object_sub_type elements within
object type definitions which themselves are object sub-types. An object type hierarchy
can be as deep as required by the protocol being defined.
The ordering of an object type relative to other object types in the same hierarchy or subhierarchy when drawn in the timeline display or lists is determined by the value of the
relative_display_order attribute for each object type. The order of columns in the timeline
display is determined in the same manner for top-level object types.
This is shown in the following figure:
Figure 32

Ordering of Top-Level Object Types Using "relative_display_order" Attributes

Note that the integer values for the attributes do not have to be sequential. You can leave
"space" between these values. This makes it easy to add new top-level object types at a
later date, if needed.
The top-level object types can be placed in any order, it is recommended that the most
abstract top-level object types be placed in the left-most column and that other columns
be placed in order of decreasing level of abstraction. This encourages debug to start with
the highest level of abstract possible. Proceed to more detailed information as needed to
analyze the protocol activity.

Object Type Fields or Attributes
When debugging protocol-related data, information about the objects that were generated
during simulation is very important. This information includes the types of those objects,
the start and end times of those objects, and the relationships between the objects.
However, perhaps the most important information that is required for tracking down

Object Type Fields or Attributes

the details of a protocol-related issue comes from the field values (or attribute values)
associated with each object.
Field (or attribute) definitions are associated with an object type. The specification of fields
is related to the object type hierarchy. Object sub-types can specify values for fields that
are defined in their parent object type declaration. In other words, the lowest-level object
types in an object type hierarchy inherit the field definitions of the parent object types all
the way up the object type hierarchy tree.
An object type is usually associated with a particular SystemVerilog class. if this is the
case, each field for that object type is usually associated with a particular data member of
that class.
The field element defines an object type field using the attributes shown in the following
table:

name

The name to use when referring to the field. This name
is also used as the display text for the field

data_type

The type declaration for the field using SystemVerilog
syntax. Examples of this are bit, bit [7:0], int, and so on

While the ability to capture and display the values of object fields is an important aspect of
protocol debugging, it is necessary that the attributes be typed to fully take advantage of
the Verdi Protocol Analyzer protocol-oriented debugging environment. In other words, it is
desirable to indicate whether the type of a field is, for example, an integer, a [simulation]
time, a floating-point number, a bit-vector or a string.
The typing of attributes is important. It enables sophisticating searching and filtering
capabilities. For example, applying comparison operators (such as `<' and `>') to an
attribute whose values are represented as strings can produce completely different results
than applying the same operators to an attribute (with the same values) whose values are
represented as integers.
SystemVerilog data types enable type-based searches that use comparison operators
in the same manner as those comparison operators would operate in the context of a
simulation.
However, the Verdi Protocol Analyzer does not recognize every SystemVerilog type. In
the case that the specified data type for a field is not supported, the values for that field
are interpreted as strings. Perhaps the most common situation in which this occurs is for
field values that are defined using enumerated types. Even when enumerated type values
are interpreted as strings, it is still possible to perform sophisticated searches using those
fields.

Note that object type field definitions share some structural characteristics with object type

Signal Interface Groups
While the Verdi Protocol Analyzer provides debug and analysis capabilities at a level
of abstraction that is above the waveform view, there are times when it is necessary to
examine the detailed bus activity at the signal interface level, especially in the case of
debugging protocol-related errors. However, a waveform view of the bus interface signals
on its own is often difficult to understand, as such, a view typically contains a large amount
of information with little context regarding what bus-related activity is occurring and when.
To address this challenge, the Verdi Protocol Analyzer can be synchronized with the Verdi
waveform viewer to help correlate the protocol-level representation of the bus activity

Signal Interface Groups

presented in the Protocol Analyzer timeline display with the signal-level representation of
the bus signal interface presented in a wave window.
To use this capability, the simulation of the design must have been run in a manner
that captures signal change information (that is, using $fsdbDumpvars, or some other
equivalent mechanism).
As discussed earlier in this document, signal interface groups can be associated with a
protocol extension definition.
The signal interface groups are used to populate the Verdi nWave window with particular
interface signals that are associated with the protocol. Multiple signal interface groups can
be supplied with the protocol extension definition.
This can be useful if the protocol supports multiple interfaces or if there are situations
where it is beneficial to load only a subset of the protocol interface signals into the
waveform window.
Interface signals are added to the wave window as defined by one or more signal interface
groups. A protocol extension can include multiple signal interface definitions.
For example, the extension definition for the AXI protocol includes a number of different
signal groups to provide the end user with a choice of signal interface definitions (for
example, read interface signals, write interface signals, and address interface signals).
Keep in mind that the signal interface groups are used to display protocol-related signals
and thus are specific to the protocol.
The signal_if_group element defines a signal interface group using the attributes shown in
the following table:

if_name

The name of the interface with which the signal group is associated.
If the signal interface group is associated with multiple interfaces,
multiple interfaces can be specified using "," as the delimiter

group_name

The name to use when referring to the signal interface group. This
name cannot contain any spaces or non-alphanumeric characters,
with the exception of underscore (`_') characters. For simplicity, the
use of all lower-case letters is recommended

display_text

The text to display when information pertaining to the signal
interface group is shown within the UI

description

A brief (usually one-line) description of the signal interface group
(this can provide clarity to the user within the UI, if needed)

Signal Interface Groups

extended_interface_p
ath

If VIP clients are unable to capture the complete path for the signal
interface group, this option path can be specified. If specified, the
value of this attribute is appended to the interface paths that were
captured during simulation (described later) and then attempt to find
signals from the appended path.

signals

The list of signals which are associated with the group. If a particular
radix should be used when displaying the signal in nWave, one
or more radix specifiers can be included in square brackets ("[ ]")
following each signal name. Multiple radix specifiers can be listed
using "," as the delimiter.

An example of a signal interface group for the AXI protocol is shown below. Note that
signal interface groups are immediate sub-elements of the top protocol element. Other
details of the protocol definition have been removed or truncated for clarity.
<protocol >
<!-AXI Tcl File (Signal Interface Group) Definitions -->
<signal_if_group>
if_name="svt_axi_master_if,svt_axi_slave_if"
name="read_address"
display_text="Read Address"
description="Displays the read address signals"
signals="arvalid, arready, arid, araddr, arlen, arsize, arburst,
arlock, arcache, arprot, ardomain, arsnoop, arbar,
read_addr_xact_num[decimal, unsigned]"

/>

</protocol>

Integration Steps
This section describes the steps that are required to integrate a VIP using VC Apps
Protocol Analyzer. The following are the five integration steps:
1. Analysis of the VIP and creation of an initial protocol extension definition
This process includes the following sub-steps:
Identification of the object type hierarchies that can be captured in the VIP.
For each object type, identification of the fields that are associated with that type.
Creation of a skeleton protocol extension definition for the VIP that includes the
object types and fields identified in the previous two steps.
Validation of the structure and the contents of the initial protocol extension definition
(by setting the PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH environment variable and examining the
protocol definition in the Protocols tab of the Verdi Protocol Analyzer).
2. Modification of the VIP SystemVerilog code to create a Protocol Analyzer writer
and capture the objects of interest along with their associated fields (that is,
attributes)
This process includes the following sub-steps:
Analysis of the structure of the VIP and modification to include and import the VC
Apps Protocol Analyzer writer.
Analysis of the structure of the VIP and modification to create a writer (if requested).
For each object to be captured, the object must first be created when it starts.
For each object, each field value must be captured for that object at the appropriate
location in the VIP code.
Each object must be ended at the appropriate location in the VIP code.
3. Modification of the build or the simulation environment to enable successful
compilation and simulation of the design
This step primarily requires modification of the SystemVerilog compiler include path
and specification of the location of the Verdi library.
4. Modification of the environment to enable invocation of the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer
This step requires modification of the execution environment. This step is also quite
simple and primarily requires specification of the location of the Verdi libraries. Also,
before invoking the Verdi Protocol Analyzer, the PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH environment

Creating a Protocol Extension Definition

variable must be set to point to the location of the required protocol extension
definitions.
5. Tuning of the protocol extension
This step in the process is the tuning of the protocol extension. This process is
intended to prompt a general review of the protocol extension definition. This step likely
includes modification of the object type colors to make the viewing of simulation results
more pleasing to the eye (often it is difficult to surmise ahead of time whether colors
clash when they appear next to each other).

Creating a Protocol Extension Definition
The apb block is relatively simple. It has a top-level agent that instantiates a monitor
sub-block. The monitor sub-block detects READ or WRITE transactions. Each of these
transactions has two fields: a 32-bit address field and a 32-bit data field.
The protocol extension definition should include two different object types. These object
types are used to distinguish between the READ transactions and WRITE transactions.
This enables the Protocol Analyzer to represent the transactions using different text
and colors. It also enables the differentiation between these types of transactions when
performing searches or examining summary information.
It is desirable to have these transactions rendered in a single column. Therefore, the
object types for READ and WRITE transactions should both be sub-types of a top-level
transaction object type.
Also, since READ and WRITE transactions both use the address and data fields, these
fields should be associated with this top-level transaction type. This approach avoids
having copies of these field definitions for the two object sub-types. It results in a clean
object type definitions. It also simplifies searching for all transactions with a particular
address or data value.

The code includes two conditional (that is, if) statements. The first conditional statement
checks if the writer is null.
If the writer is null, the code checks the local context of the configuration database for the
enable_pa_writer bit attribute. If this attribute is found and is set to 1, a local instance
of the writer is created for version 1.0 of the uvm_apb protocol. The instance path that is
passed to the writer's constructor is created by taking the path to the agent and appending
.mon (to indicate that the monitor component is collecting data). However, whether or not
.mon should be appended to the instance path is purely an implementation decision).
The final lines of code in this first conditional block checks the local context of the
configuration database for the apb_if_path attribute. If this attribute is found, it is added
to the list of interface paths for this instance of the VIP.
There are a number of different ways that the interface path can be passed to the VIP.
Firstly, note that the interface path is different from the VIP hierarchy path. The interface
path comes from the location where the interface is instantiated in the design, which is
often at the top level. The configuration database is a handy mechanism for capturing that
information in another block in the design hierarchy, but have that information be available
to instances of the VIP using a general, reusable approach. In this example, the name of
the attribute (apb_if_path) is arbitrarily chosen.
The important point is that this attribute is added to the configuration database in the code

to instances of the VIP using a general, reusable approach. In this example, the name of
the attribute (apb_if_path) is arbitrarily chosen.
The important point is that this attribute is added to the configuration database in the code
where the interface is instantiated (more on this later), so that the instance of the VIP

can retrieve that path (and add it to the writer) no matter where the VIP ended up being
instantiated in the test environment hierarchy.
The second conditional statement also checks if the writer is null. If the writer is not null, it
is passed to the instance of the apb_monitor component by calling the set_pa_writer
method for the monitor class.
The monitor component includes the code that actually detects READ and WRITE
transactions. Thus, it is the appropriate class for adding the code that uses the VC Apps
Protocol Analyzer writer object to record protocol activity.
In a manner almost identical to the agent class, the apb_monitor.sv file must be
updated to store an instance. It is passed to the monitor from the agent. In addition, the
monitor class must be updated to record READ and WRITE transactions (along with their
associated attributes). This requires modifying two parts of the file, the first of which is
shown in the following figure:
The following two items are added to this file:
* One item declares the VC Apps Protocol Analyzer writer object.
* The other item defines a function for setting the writer instance.
These two items have been highlighted using light red shading in the following figure:

The second set of modifications are done to the run phase of the monitor, as shown in the
following figure:

There are three basic steps that are performed in the modified code when an object is
recorded:
* If the writer is not null, create an object using the appropriate object type name, the
channel name (if applicable), and the start time for the object (if earlier than the current
time)
* If the object is successfully created, add attributes to the object when their values are
known. This code is repeated for each attribute to be recorded.
* When the end time of the object is reached (assuming that the object was initially
created successfully), end the object.
Depending upon how many types of objects are being captured (and the structure of the
VIP code), this general object processing pattern might be repeated in the code multiple
times. However, in this example, both READ and WRITE transactions are detected in one
location, so this pattern appears only once. The modifications to the code are highlighted
using light red shading.
The first major block of code first checks if objects should be recorded (that is, if the writer
is not null). If so, the object type name is set according to the APB transaction type. Note
that the two possible values (apb_read_transaction and apb_write_transaction)
match the names of object types defined in the protocol extension.
Using this name, a new object is created by calling the create_object method of the writer
class . This method returns an object uid (unique identifier), which is a string that is used
4. For more information about VC Apps Protocol Analyzer writer methods, refer to the appendix that lists and
describes all of the methods available in the VC Apps Protocol Analyzer writer API.

to reference the object in later operations. If an empty string is returned, there is an error
creating the object (in which case the error is reported in the simulation log).
If the object is successfully created, the addr attribute is set for the object by calling the
set_object_attribute_bit_vector method of the writer class. This attribute is set at this point
in the code, as the address is known and fixed.
In general, it is recommended that attributes be set when their values are known and fixed
(as opposed to setting the values of all attributes at the time an object ends). Using this
approach, if an unexpected error stops the simulation before it can complete cleanly, those
attribute values that are recorded are available to potentially help track down the source of
the error.
The second major block of code sets the data attribute for the object. Finally, the third
major block of code ends the object.
There is one topic that is not yet described: capturing interface paths and adding the paths
to the configuration database.
This operation is performed in the tb_top.sv file in the codec sub-directory. This file
contains the code that instantiates the interfaces.

Two lines of code are added to this file:
1. The first line specifies the hierarchical design path for the APB interface
2. The second line specifies the hierarchical design path for the (codec) "VIP" interface.
Since the name of the top-level module is tb_top and the interfaces are directly
instantiated within this module, the paths to these two interfaces are known and can be
directly added to the configuration database.
This is a simple example of adding the paths to the database; other mechanisms might
be available to the verification engineer, based on the overall structure of the verification
environment. For example, if the test environment uses a general configuration object
that already contains handles to the interfaces, the underlying VIP code could extract the
configuration object and get the path to the interface directly.

Configuration Control Considerations

Protocols Tab Showing the "UVM APB" Protocol Extension Definition

Configuration Control Considerations
In the apb example, there is a single configuration database attribute that controls whether
or not to enable the recording of objects. As this component only records one kind of
activity, the use of a single attribute to control recording is appropriate. However, for some
VIPs, it is useful to provide a more granular set of controls to determine what kind of data
is recorded.
Some items to consider are as follows:
* The ability to enable or disable object recording (global).
* The ability to enable or disable object capture based on object types, protocol layers,
and so on.
* The ability to control the amount of data that is captured.
* The ability to make mid simulation configuration changes.
As previously mentioned, any recording method, no matter how optimized has some
impact on simulation performance. In general, the level of impact is difficult to quantify.
This is because the impact depends on several factors:
* The complexity of the protocol.
* The capabilities of the VIP (Verification IP).
* The extent of instrumentation, such as how many objects are recorded.
* The number and type of attributes that are recorded for each object.

Important Rules for Creating Objects
When an object is created using the create_object method of the VC Apps Protocol
Analyzer API, the object type must be specified. However, in some VIPs under certain
conditions, it is not possible to know the type of the object at the time the transaction is
intended to start. Sometimes it takes one or more additional clock cycles to determine the
object type, especially if the protocol extension defines a complex object type hierarchy.
The create_object method supports this situation, by providing an optional object start
time that is earlier than the current simulation time.
Note:
The use of this feature, while occasionally necessary, is highly discouraged.
Before utilizing this capability, a thorough analysis of the VIP should be
performed. This analysis helps determine if it is possible to remedy this situation
by making changes to the VIP code. If this is not possible, it is imperative to
ensure that the rules described in this section are never violated.
Even if these rules are carefully followed, the use of this feature introduces
some impact on performance.

text:
In the scenario on the left ,Scenario 1, no other time is specified in the call to
create_object. The start time for each of the objects is equal to the current simulation
time. This is the preferred method for creating objects.
The other two scenarios (labeled Scenario 2 and Scenario 3), show situations where both
of the objects are created specifying a start time that is earlier than the current simulation
time. This earlier time is referred to as the write-back time.
The rule that cannot be violated is: As objects are created the order of the object start
times must be maintained. In the previous figure, that is, the following must be true: 2B
>= 2A. By taking this rule into consideration, it should become clear why the situation
illustrated by Scenario 2 is permitted, however the situation illustrated by Scenario 3
violates this rule.
This rule only applies in the following two situations:
* This rule applies to objects that have the same object type in the same channel, when
channels are specified for objects of that type.
* It also applies to objects that have the same object type, when channels are not
specified for objects of that type.

Writer Macros or Defines
ENABLE_VERDI_PA_WRITER
This directive must be defined to enable the functionality defined in the VC Apps Protocol
Analyzer writer class. The intent of this macro is to allow the compilation and use of the
VIP outside of the Verdi environment. By default, this macro is not defined.

VERDI_PA_WRITER_BV_MAX_WIDTH
This macro defines the maximum width of a bit-vector that can be written to the FSDB. If
this macro is not explicitly defined by the user, the value for this macro is set to 1024.
See the set_object_attribute_value_bit_vector method for additional details.

This method ends a protocol object. When this method is called, the end time of the
object is set to the current simulation time. At this point, all information about the object
is considered to be specified. Thus, no further changes can be made to the attributes
associated with the object.
